Agriculture Canada is predicting that realized net income for Saskatchewan farmers for this year will be about 30 per cent below the 10-year average and the 1993 forecast is set for a realized net income of only $238 million or about $4,000 per farmer. We have a serious crisis on our hands that must be addressed.
As the rally indicated, we need the injection of cash but we also need the protection of the Wheat Board and the security that the maintenance of the Crow benefit provides to all the producers in Saskatchewan. Without the maintenance of these longer term programs the other policies are simply band-aids that will eventually fall off and create the damage we are trying to prevent.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity on this opposition day to participate in this debate. It stems from a New Democratic Party motion which is critical of government policies toward agriculture.
In part, I would like to address that motion from the perspective of a member of Parliament who represents an area which is indeed as grain dependent as any part of the country. It is the southwestern and the south and central part of Saskatchewan which consists of some
25,000	square miles. I have 9,000 to 10,000 of the farmers in Saskatchewan and probably about 20 per cent of the viable farming operations.
I spent the first three weeks in January travelling around my constituency. I met with rural municipal councils. I met with groups of 6, 8 and 10 producers here and there. I tried to do this, quite frankly, in the absence of the representatives of the so-called organizations of whatever stripe. I tried to get away from them and just talk with farmers at the grass roots.
I fear that sometimes when the farm organizations come with policies, they are at a national level, or at the very least at a regional level. I am not entirely satisfied that they speak for all of their members. That was the reason for trying to get right down to the grass roots. I can attest to the fact that there is an enormous amount of frustration, disappointment and despondency out there.
First, I want to talk in terms of the history of the prairie grain sector. Then I will talk about the reality
which it faces today, the politics of it and the hope that maybe there are some solutions and answers out there.
This is a relatively young sector of our economy. The prairies were for the most part settled in the early 1900s. It was a deliberate policy to settle and to populate the west. The offer was made throughout the world that people could come to Canada. They came on the promise of free land. They came as well for the kind of opportunities and freedoms which our country has and maintains proudly to this day.
People came from the northern United States, eastern Canada, Scandinavia, the British Isles, Germany, Ukraine, Poland and literally from the four comers of the earth. They came to settle the prairies.
It is very interesting and almost unparalleled in history that the country was laid out ahead of time. It was surveyed into sections or square miles and townships which consist of areas 6 miles by 6 miles, or 36 square miles. It was all laid out ahead of time and when the homesteaders came they had the opportunity to file for a particular quarter section of land. It was theirs provided they broke it up and cultivated a certain portion of that ground. They had the opportunity to build on it.
The information indicates that the number of farms peaked at a fairly early time during this century. I believe that in Saskatchewan, there were around 100,000 farms in the 1920s and 1930s and that the average farm size was in the area of 350 to 400 acres. If one follows that sort of chart, one will see that the number of farms has been steadily declining ever since those peak years. That decline continues today.
One will see as well that there is a corresponding increase in the size of the farms, which are now in the area of about 1,100 acres.
The west was laid out before the people came. It was the era of the steam engine. There were places for the train to take on water every five or six miles and it was around those spots that towns and villages grew up. That is where the grain elevators were constructed and that is where the farmers would haul their grain to the elevator so it could later be shipped out by rail to tide water and on to export.
There was a long and glorious history where the prairies were the bread basket of the world. There were
February 9, 1993

huge markets in Europe that the prairies were able to satisfy. These were the golden years. Wheat was the king of the grains.
These villages and towns developed every five or six miles along the railway tracks. Farmers hauled maybe 20-25 bushels of wheat to the elevator in a horse-drawn wagon in the very early days. Those days are long gone and the reason for that is not a trade war today. It is the march of history. It is technology and advances in machinery and equipment. It is road building, communication and technology. It may have taken that pioneer farmer all day to take a load of grain to the elevator a mile or two away. Now they move a trailer of grain-huge amounts of grain-vast distances in that time.
The end result has been a consolidation. Many of these small towns and villages have ceased to exist and many more, I am sad to say, are in their death throes. It is not because of a particular policy of a government of any stripe. I say this not in any partisan way. It is simply reality. It is a result of technology and of markets.
I do not think there is much use in clinging to the old myth of the role of government to preserve rural Canada as it might have been or as someone idyllically remembers it 40 or 50 years ago when the population was at its peak. I am not so sure that those days were particularly rosy anyway. Oldtimers tell me that they do not recall so many wonderful times.
I guess the bottom line is that this movement from the rural areas to the urban ones is something that is a result of technology. It is happening in Saskatchewan. It has happened across Canada. It has happened world-wide.
We are told that back in the 1930s something like a third of all Canadians lived on the farm. Today I think that figure is in the area of perhaps 3 per cent or 4 per cent.
Over the past number of years, many programs have been generated to try to deal with the problems of agriculture. It is not easy to do because agriculture speaks with many voices. Sometimes people who live in the north see things differently from those who live in the south. Those who live in the west naturally see things differently from those who live in the east. If one is into livestock, one sees things differently than one would if one was a straight grain farmer.
Supply
There is an enormous difficulty in devising and developing national programs that work and that are seen to be satisfactory to all concerned.
In the past, it has been shown that programs like area-based crop insurance, like the WGSA which triggered huge areas and which had a five-year rolling average which turned out to be inadequate at the time when it was most needed. These programs have been discarded and a new generation of safety-net programs have been brought forward.
These programs, GRIP and NISA, were not developed in isolation. They were the result of many months and, indeed, many years of work, not just by federal and provincial governments, but by producer groups and by individual farmers. They were designed to try to overcome the obvious shortcomings of some of the programs that preceded them.
Those safety-net programs are in their infancy at this time. There are problems with them, yet at the same time they do seem to be working across most of the country. There are some criteria such as individuality, certainty, predictability and bankability that were central to these programs.
It is an unfortunate fact that GRIP has not been allowed to work within the province of Saskatchewan, which is a major grain-growing sector of the country. It is one of the sources of enormous frustration as related to me by producers within my constituency.
Over the past number of years, a variety of government programs have delivered unprecedented support into the grains and oilseeds sector. I believe that the numbers for Saskatchewan, for example, over the last six or seven years average out to something like slightly over $20,000 in support from the federal government to each farm operation within the province of Saskatchewan.
The irony is that for the taxpayer obviously it is too much. Yet for the hard-pressed producer who has been buffeted by historically low grain prices owing to subsidies beyond our borders it is not enough. So we have this fundamental problem. It is reality.
Canada is up against the United States and the European Community in this subsidy war. These countries have large populations, they have deep pockets and they have a much smaller dependence on export than Canada does.

February 9, 1993
Supply
Canada has 27 million people. We try to export five out of every six bushels of wheat that we grow. Eighty-three per cent of our production has to go outside of Canada hopefully to a willing buyer who has some money to pay us for our product. Unfortunately, at this point in time there are not those buyers out there and where there are buyers, the price is being undermined by the export subsidies and the domestic subsidies of our competing countries.
The United States has a population of about 250 million people and the European Common Market has about 330 million. Their dependency on export is much less. In the case of the United States it is 45 per cent. In the case of the Common Market it is something less than 20 per cent.
We are in the situation where the Canadian taxpayer, on a per capita basis, is putting more into the grain sector than his counterpart in the United States or in Europe. Sad to say, it is still not enough. What is the answer?
The Prairie Pools Organization presented a recent brief, December 1, 1992, to federal cabinet ministers. There was one particular paragraph which simply leaped out at me: "We cannot compete indefinitely with the export subsidies and trade-distorting internal support programs which are used by other major grain and oilseed trading countries, which are far in excess of those available to Canadian producers".
That is absolutely correct. It sums up the problem in a nutshell. If this is to go on indefinitely we cannot compete with the treasuries of those other nations. We simply do not have the resources available. That leads to a lot of the frustration and I guess to a lot of the politics.
I recall being at farm rallies in Rosetown, which is in Saskatchewan, Regina and Winnipeg in the fall of 1991.1 was also in Shaunavon and Regina in the spring of 1992, in North Battleford last fall and of course more recently in Saskatoon. I have listened very carefully at those rallies and of course I understand and hear clearly the frustration.
I understand that there is a need there. We have people who are dependent on growing of wheat for a living. The question is how long we can continue to grow that wheat for export when there are no willing buyers out there and where there are, they are unable or
unwilling to pay the necessary price. That is the reality that we face. What can we do about it?
I do not think it is good enough for opposition parties to come in here and try to deal with this problem through a cheap, grandstanding sort of motion like the one that is in front of the House today. I heard my colleague from Algoma, the Liberal agriculture critic, giving the old-style 1960s approach to this thing. There was not a single useful suggestion. It was just a long litany of the problems. God knows, we all know them. The people on the farms know them. They are not interested in hearing about that.
What they want to talk about are some useful, sensible solutions or alternatives, given the circumstances and given the reality out there. Then we have their friends in the New Democratic Party, the guys with two heads. They have one head for Ottawa and one head for Saskatchewan. Here in Ottawa we have heard some of it already and we are going to hear more during the course of the day. There is no expenditure which would be too great for the Saskatchewan grain farmers. They need help and the government had better go out, borrow a bunch of money and give it to them.
Meanwhile, back in Saskatchewan, guess what? They have a New Democratic government in Saskatchewan that has completely and utterly turned its back on the number one industry in Saskatchewan, agriculture.
This motion today has to be without a doubt the single most hypocritical motion that has ever been presented on the floor of the House of Commons. An NDP government in Saskatchewan which tore up the national GRIP program, unilaterally and arbitrarily tore up a program, did it retroactively, breached contracts which thousands of farmers had signed in good faith and then passed legislation retroactively saying that they were not responsible for the breach of contracts. They then had the audacity to say that it is somehow the fault of Ottawa that the safety net program is not working. Lo and behold, on top of that they have the unmitigated gall, the audacity, to come into this House today and try to point a finger at a federal government which has provided-unprecedented albeit; maybe it is not enough but it is unprecedented-support for that sector at the same time
February 9, 1993

as their brethren, their friends in Saskatchewan are saying: "Sorry, we do not have any money for you".
Agriculture is a shared jurisdiction. I do not think it is good enough for New Democrats to whine here in Ottawa about the federal government's role while at the same time they have offered nothing, absolutely nothing, for agriculture within the province of Saskatchewan.
I view it as being two-faced and hypocritical. I am not going to say more about that. At the end of the day producers are frustrated. What they are seeing in their minds is a tennis match going back and forth. The ball is bouncing between levels of government.
At the rally in Saskatoon many farmers called for a mediation process to try to get federal and provincial governments together to try to fix the GRIP safety net problem in Saskatchewan. I do not blame them for feeling that way. The federal government and the federal minister are ready, willing and able to sit down with the provincial counterpart to try to fix the problem which was caused and created by the New Democratic Party in the first place.
In the brief time I have left I did want to touch on a number of suggestions that I have, given the circumstances, given the reality that there is no market and that the return at the moment is coming from the taxpayer. One questions whether it can come forever from the taxpayer. Obviously, more efficiencies are needed. There has been a lot of discussion about that and work being done on it.
Western Diversification: A $1.2 billion fund established by the federal government to do exactly what its name implies, to try to diversify a western Canadian economy which is all too dependent on grain.
Lower interest rates: the policies of our government trying to contain government spending, trying to contain the kind of philosophy and attitude that was left here from 20 years of Liberal government, we are succeeding here. That is why we have stable inflation and lower interest rates, the greatest gift I think that we can give not just to agriculture but to small business as well.
In addition, we are negotiating internationally, negotiating at the GATT and bilaterally with other countries,
Supply
at the same time trying to secure a lessening of these harmful subsidies which have caused the problem.
Finally, we need co-operation federally and provincially to try to make the farm safety net programs work. In that regard, I urge my colleagues in the NDP here to stop complaining about Ottawa, go back to Regina and ask your provincial counterparts in good faith to sit down and see if we cannot make things work for Canadian producers.

Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in the hon. gentleman's speech. I think he chose wisely to concentrate on the changes that have occurred and the difficulties of adapting to change.
Toward the end of his speech he also talked about hypocrisy, claiming that the NDP members were speaking one set of truths in Ottawa and another set in Saskatchewan. I think for the record he ought to know if he continues with his clear eyed analysis that he attempted at the beginning of his speech, the reason there is the problem in Saskatchewan as a result of the shortfall in the income in 1992 has nothing to do with the change in policy precipitated by the provincial government bill last April.
That shortfall in income is a direct result of the problems with the program that was initiated between the federal and the then Conservative government of Saskatchewan for the 1991 GRIP program which paid out its payments in 1992.
We have not begun to reap any of the shortage or benefits from the NDP induced program that was begun last spring, so he should get that clear when he is describing the problem. The problem that farmers have is because the original GRIP was not adequate.
As a second point he talked about the problems of inducing change and how farmers are going to have to change because the Russians do not have credit to buy wheat anymore and the U.S. has been systematically interfering in international prices to depress the price by as much as $80 per tonne.
He should be aware that the program that was introduced last spring in Saskatchewan would in fact let market forces occur and would in fact encourage diversification to other crops. It has forced a big chunk of Saskatchewan's farmers to look for other markets in the Third World and Europe for products like lentils, pul-

Supply
ses-peas and beans for most of us-and the the various oilseed crops that we have been diversifying into for a long time. The payments by crop district instead of on an individual basis will in fact encourage that.
I think he should perhaps give credit for applying his own ideas to that provincial government for the changes that were proposed in the spring of 1992 which will be felt in the income of 1993. For some people it will not be a good feeling.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I may be confused but I thought the hon. member had already made a speech during this debate. I am wondering how it is he is allowed to make a second one.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I hope that the hon. member will end his remarks and ask a question of the previous speaker.

Mr. Speaker, it should be obvious to the hon. member who has been here for some time that this is a period for comments and questions and that is what I am doing.
There have been two questions. The third comment is that while agriculture is a shared jurisdiction, the federal responsibility for trade, which is what got us into the financial problem that we are in, is all in the federal government's court. The shortfall because of the trade wars that have befallen Canada's farmers should be borne by the federal government. As a lawyer, he should know that the provincial government is only responsible under the Constitution for the production side only.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to respond in the limited time available. I heard what the hon. member had to say about the GRIP. I was in Shaunavon, Regina, North Battleford and Saskatoon at the rallies and I know what I heard. I have listened to farmers in my area and I know exactly what they think of those unilateral and arbitrary changes that were made to the GRIP by the hon. member's socialist friends in Saskatchewan who have abandoned the grain sector.
The most vital sector of the Saskatchewan economy was abandoned completely by the hon. member's party. They have the gross hypocrisy to come in here and complain about the federal government's role.
It was interesting that GRIP, a national program with national standards, is working in Alberta and Manitoba. At the rally in Saskatoon, the usual National Farmers Union people were crowded around the microphones at ten o'clock in the morning much, I might add, to the chagrin of the wheat pool organizers. People from a couple of plants in Alberta came in to complain about GRIP in Alberta. But the fact is that GRIP is working reasonably well in the other provinces of this country. The reason it is not working in Saskatchewan is because the NDP government, cohorts of these people who brought this motion today, refuse to give it a chance to work.
In the few moments I have left I want to make some constructive suggestions to the provincial government of Saskatchewan. My hon. friend mentioned trade. I think it is high time that the NDP stop whining about the CUSTA, NAFTA and GATT. I think it is time they recognized the fact that Saskatchewan above all is a trading province and that we have negotiated very important access to the United States market, as well as a dispute settlement mechanism which has been tested and found to work time and time again. It worked for pork and now for wheat. "Canada wins wheat dispute with the United States", today's paper states.
That agreement has given important access to other Saskatchewan producers in livestock and beef and pork. These people who are criticizing trade agreements should go to Saskatchewan and explain that to the cattlemen and the pork producers.
I would like to make three brief points. I think it is important that there be co-operation between the federal and provincial agriculture ministers on the GRIP. Second, the province could harmonize the PST and the GST and lift the burden of sales tax from the inputs of Saskatchewan farm producers. I urge that they do that.
Finally, maybe they have to stand up to the big public sector unions in Saskatchewan which really are their political bosses. We in Ottawa did stand up to PSAC and the other public sector unions. We froze wages because it
February 9, 1993

had to be done. I challenge them to do the same in Saskatchewan. I do not think they have the gumption to do it. It is a matter of priorities.

Mr. Speaker, I have a short question for the hon. member who, as he said, was in Saskatoon at the rally. The biggest response at the rally in Saskatoon, the biggest ovation, was when one speaker got up and said: "Leave the wheat board alone".
I would like to ask this member if he thinks that barley should remain under the sole jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. Second, does he agree with the New Democratic Party that before any changes are made to the Canadian Wheat Board it should be put to a vote so that all the producers can have a say in what they want to happen to their own wheat board? Does the member agree with that position? Does he think that barley should remain under the sole jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board as the farmers in Saskatoon said it should?

Mr. Speaker, in brief, first of all I find it impossible to agree with the New Democratic Party. I want to make that perfectly clear. I disagree violently with the method of operation and with the hypocrisy of coming in with a motion like this today when they have abjectly failed producers in the province of Saskatchewan.
Second, with regard to barley the hon. member knows that there is a study being undertaken at the present time. I am perfectly willing to wait for the results of that to see what it says. I know as well that a number of producers in my area are concerned about what they see as the dumping of some of our product into Montana, into the northern part of the United States, which is of concern to them. They are frustrated and upset with the wheat board over this and with a major farm organization.
I do not have time to go into it at this point, but I can say that there are quite legitimate concerns out there among many producers about the monopolistic situation. That is not to say that it will be changed, but I cannot believe that it is not possible in a democracy like Canada to at least discuss intelligently some options.
Supply
If there are some problems with these organizations and with these institutions, let us be up front about it and talk about some of these problems to see if we can solve them in a co-operative manner.

Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to share part of my time with the hon. member for Gatineau.
The motion before this House condemns the government for reneging on its commitment to Canadian farmers by changing policy. This motion identifies the areas of uncertainty that prevail in Canadian agriculture and the continuing erosion of net farm income.
Let me put this into perspective. Three years ago the Minister of Agriculture started talking about farm family income and used figures that painted a very rosy picture. I pointed out these misleading figures last Thursday night at a farm rally in Lucknow, Ontario, where the community centre was jammed full. Incidentally this meeting was organized by a group of farmers calling themselves "Line in the Dirt". They drew a line in the dirt and said: "Enough is enough". That was back in 1991 and things have not changed.
In 1991 the so-called average Canadian farm family income was $39,638, but that is very misleading because more than half of it came from income earned from other sources than the farming operation. For example, if the spouse was teaching school, nursing, working in an office in town or working in a factory, that was called farm family income. The non-related income was added to farm income.
This left a balance of $17,115 of income from the farming operation itself. Of that amount, $9,927 was a government subsidy, both federal and provincial. When we deduct these subsidies from the net farm income of $17,115 that leaves a balance of $7,188 of income from the actual sale of farm products. Slightly more than 20 per cent of the so-called farm family income came from the sale of farm products. I submit that is a national disgrace.
Food production and processing have to be made matters of national security. Canadian consumers pay the second lowest amount for their food in terms of disposable income of any country in the world for the highest quality food in the world. The ironic part of this is that others in the food chain, particularly the food distribution sector, are doing very well. I refer to The Globe and Mail Report on Business showing the average five-year rate of return on capital invested in the food

February 9, 1993
Supply
distribution industry to be 17.2 per cent from 1986 to 1990. For the same period Canadian banks had a 13.3 per cent return and Canadian agriculture had a return of 6.2 per cent. This was not even enough to cover the interest on their loans.
Poultry and dairy producers were included in that 6.2 per cent figure, and they had a return of between 8 per cent and 9 per cent and have been criticized for doing so.
A few years ago this government took away the two-price wheat system that served this nation very well since the early 1970s. This program served Canadians very well for many years. In terms of higher world prices, the domestic price provided protection for our consumers, and the producers of Canada received lower prices for the products used domestically. However in times of low world prices it provided a higher price to producers for the product used domestically.
Our studies show that this policy was discontinued. At that time the net producer prices for wheat tumbled in Canada. The price of consumer products manufactured from wheat did not drop but rather continued to escalate. From 1982 to 1992 the value of wheat declined by 31 per cent and the price of a box of soda crackers increased to 25 times the farm gate price of wheat.
Last year an eight-ounce box of Breton Wheat crackers, made in Canada, sold for 99 cents U.S. in South Carolina and sold in Canada within a range from $2.69 to $2.89, the average being $2.79. There were 3 cents worth of wheat in that box. Ten days ago I bought an eight-ounce box of these crackers in Chilliwack, B.C., again containing 3 cents worth of wheat, for $3.15. That is an increase of 36 cents a box since last summer. If Canadian farmers were to receive 6 cents out of that 36-cent increase, they would be satisfied, could survive and make an acceptable living.
I am not sure I am supposed to show this in the House, but I want to draw your attention to it, Mr. Speaker. It is a national disgrace that people make returns like that and farmers have to depend on government handouts to
make a living that is not commensurate with that of the rest of society.
I was speaking last August to a person in the food distribution business. I asked him for an explanation of the increases at a time when farm prices were deteriorating. He admitted that in some sectors the prices and the profits were exorbitant. This situation is absurd. Canadian farmers need subsidies to hang on and have to find off-farm work to put food on their own tables, and others in the processing and distribution sector are making exorbitant profits.
A recent consultant's study pointed out that five major food distributors in Canada control 80 per cent of food sales. That was in 1992, and it was up from 69 per cent in 1987. On the surface it appeared to be adequate competition, but if we examine where these distributors operate within Canada, some regions of Canada have very little competition, particularly western Canada and Atlantic Canada.
I have a report of one of those firms. We find that in 1990 the firm sent $538.7 million in dividends back to the parent company in the U.S. and borrowed the money to do it. It sent over half a billion dollars in dividends back to the parent company in the United States at the same time governments were giving money to primary producers in order for them to survive. Also at the same time these farmers and their spouses had to find off-farm work to provide living expenses for themselves and to put food on their own tables.
This situation is intolerable and cannot continue. It is becoming obvious that a very few and very powerful transnational companies are slowly taking control of food supply in the western world. Five of these companies virtually control the world's grain trade.
There was a report prepared by the Library of Parliament for the agriculture committee of this House in May 1991. It was pointed out in this study into the U.S. commodity exchange fiasco in relation to soybeans in the fall of 1989 that two of these companies decided what the price of soybeans would be. The prices dropped by nearly $2 a bushel in the summer of 1989 and never recovered.
As these huge corporations take control of the marketplace there has to be a countervailing force in that marketplace or the price discovery mechanisms simply
February 9, 1993

will not work. I respectfully suggest there is no counterbalance in the world markets at the present time. Consequently the price discovery mechanism is not working.
On December 2 a news item in the Ontario Farmer pointed out that a few multinationals were jockeying for position, for dominance and control of the food industry. It went on to say that the food system in the United States resembled an hourglass with many producers and millions of consumers at either end. This was a statement by William Heffernan, head of the sociology department, Missouri State University.
I also wish to put on record that very few companies are taking more and more control of the U.S. production and food processing industry. Professor Heffernan identified the amount of control they have over production processing. For example, four firms control 69 per cent of beef processing and two of these are the same firms.
One company controls 25 per cent of chicken production and processing. It has recently bought a huge pork processing plant in Minnesota. It processes 12,000 hogs per day, 84,000 a week, more than is processed in Ontario on a weekly basis.
Of eight major commodities produced in the United States, among the top four firms one firm is listed in all eight. That is the type of competition that we are subjected to. Competition is going to wipe us out unless we as a government step in. I heard the same firm is gearing up to have two million brood sows in another midwestern state to produce its own hogs.
Yesterday I received a letter from Gerald van Koever-den from Thamesville, Ontario, who spent several years with CUSO in Thailand:
While there I worked hard to develop and implement a few strategies to enable farmers to compete and survive. This is difficult in a country where agriculture policy is completely dominated by large multinationals.
These farmers are not allowed to organize into large farm organizations and they have virtually no say at all in the process.
I submit this is starting to happen in Canada. Those few huge companies have now made Thailand the world's sixth largest exporter of poultry meat. There is extremely cheap labour in Thailand, few environmental regulations, very little supplementary heat is required
Supply
for brooding, and we suspect the export enhancement subsidized grain is used to feed the birds.
This nation needs to make food production processing a matter of national security and Canadian farmers need a fair share of the consumer food dollar. They need a return on investment, management and risk, and an income commensurate with the rest of society.

Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in the comparisons of the hon. member in the eight-ounce package of Breton biscuits. He alluded to a possible solution. He was going at it a little backward when time ran out, but he was talking about how large corporations were taking advantage of the huge differential between the farm price and the process price. I note it is very difficult for farmers to get into the next level of production so that they can capture the advantages of the processed product themselves.
I wonder if the member has any solutions as to how that might be done. In the past decade we have seen the value of farm assets drop dramatically in western Canada, and pretty precipitously in eastern Canada and central Canada. In my part of the country land prices dropped from $900 per acre down to $300 and lower, which takes a huge pool of reserve investment away from the farm community.
I note that people like dairy producers and pork producers in western Canada have made attempts to control processing. For instance, Alberta Pork Producers process most of the pork in that province through plants owned by the producers. Alberta Dairy Producers attempted to forward integrate as well by combining both the north and south Alberta dairy pools.
In both instances of pork and dairy products the provincial government kept stepping in the way and trying to stop farmers from getting into the processing business. It did not succeed with pork but it did stop the integration of the two dairy pools. The government insisted that the one in financial difficulty be sold to Beatrice Foods in the interest of avoiding a monopoly, Beatrice Foods being probably the biggest dairy in Canada and if there is anything approaching monopoly it is Beatrice Foods.
Would he tell us how he thinks farmers could avoid this interference? What does he see as possibilities for forward integration so that farmers could take advantage of these high prices for processed product?

February 9, 1993

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question. I want to hold up one example of further diversification by the prairie pools: Alberta pool, Sask pool and Manitoba pool. I also want to point out what has been happening in terms of concentration in the processing industry. I have to relate to one big firm we are referring to getting a foothold in the U.S. meat packing and other sectors of the agricultural industry. It is already in Canada. It has virtually taken over the beef industry with a huge plant in Alberta and now one in Ontario.
To see these things taking place we realize there has to be a solution. What puzzles me is the fact that quality standards in other countries do not measure up to ours. If we are to have foods imported we must make sure their quality standards measure up to ours, or else under article III of the GATT we can keep them out.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to follow on the comment about standards. I am horrified when I read what is coming through and on to our dining room tables.
Just to quote briefly, these are the kinds of chickens that are coming through. "Every week throughout the south", the southern states, "millions of chickens leaking yellow pus, stained by green faeces, contaminated by harmful bacteria or marred by lung and heart infections, cancerous tumours or skin conditions, are shipped for sale to consumers".
Another article states that according to the U.S. agriculture department, 40 per cent of all American raw poultry is contaminated. They have all sorts of gadgets where they bombard them with radioactive gamma rays to kill it.
Perhaps the member could share with the House whether our slaughtering techniques and food processing-

Mr. Speaker, indeed our standards are among the highest in the world. We would never tolerate such standards as those in Canada. In the first week of
January children became sick in Washington State from eating tainted hamburger, and some children in the Chilliwack and Abbotsford area of B.C. as well.
It is despicable those standards have been allowed to slip under deregulation of the food inspection industry in the United States. The Americans call it the SIS, the streamline inspection system. We could never allow that to happen in Canada.
My hon. friend from Parkdale-High Park is absolutely right. If they do not measure up to our standards, we must keep them out of Canada and produce our own.

Mr. Speaker, I am looking foward to attending the opening of the new Zoe Blais home this Friday, February 12, and I would like to draw your attention to the exceptional work being done by one of the community groups in my riding.
The Zoe Blais home offers moral, spiritual, material and academic support, free of charge, to 42 families in the riding of Quebec-Est. With this kind of assistance, these families will have a chance to improve their quality of life and that of their children.
I admire the initiative shown by people who value the concept of brotherhood and friendship and show this in their daily lives.
This is the kind of mutual assistance our society needs.
February 9, 1993

Mr. Speaker, the black communities across Canada are celebrating Black History Month to develop pride in their heritage and awareness in Canadians of their long history and many contributions to Canada.
Contributions of political leaders including Rosemary Brown, Emery Barnes, Lincoln Alexander, Howard McCurdy and Zanana Akande are part of this history.
In response to the Liberal leader's chief of staff who recently said that Quebec is not ready to have a black Liberal candidate, Howard McCurdy said: "In refusing to support an equality clause in the Charlottetown accord, in the exercise of veto power over candidates and in the absence of a firm policy on minority candidates, Liberals communicate a mixed message compared to the policy of inclusion of the NDP".
An NDP affirmative action policy has resulted in an historic nomination of visible minority candidates by riding associations.

Mr. Speaker, Canadian shipyards fear that Hibernia contracts to build tankers and supply vessels will be awarded to foreign competitors.
Where would be the logic? Why look to others when the work can be done right here in our own backyard? Shipyards across Canada can do the job, including the yard in Marystown which has the capability to construct the supply vessels.
In 1984 the government talked a lot about the need for a prosperous shipbuilding industry and about Canadiani-zation. Since then, thousands upon thousands of skilled shipyard workers have had their jobs wiped out. An entire industry is being threatened while the government is sitting on its hands.
I ask the government today to recognize this golden opportunity and to use the Hibernia project to help revitalize the shipbuilding industry and to provide work opportunities for its workers.

Mr. Speaker, I was appalled to read more today in The Toronto Star about the Liberal Party's candidate selection process. Apparently a Quebecer was advised not to run for a nomination because he is black.
The way the Liberal Party selects its candidates in certain ridings is distressing to many people who believe in democracy. If one of the criteria to be a candidate is race, this is even more disturbing. It is absolutely essential that everyone in this Chamber uphold the fundamental Canadian values of our Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It is not only morally wrong, it is illegal to discriminate based on race. Discrimination hurts not only individuals but all Canadians. It has no place in the candidate selection process of a political party.

Mr. Speaker, it is now almost five years since the multiculturalism act was implemented, and the government still does not know the difference between employment equity and multiculturalism.
The act should be strengthened to ensure that public service decision makers consider the diversity of Canadian society when developing policies and programs that affect all the citizens of this country.

The tabling of the annual report on the implementation of the multiculturalism act is a somewhat anti-climactic event. I believe that a non-partisan officer should review the implementation of the act.
The tendency today has been to highlight the successes instead of some of the failures of the policy. Having the

Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship review the implementation of its own act is like having the fox take care of the chickens. This situation must change.
