speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was shocked this morning when I heard that the executive assistant to the Leader of the Official Opposition had said it was not the right time for a black candidate to run in the Quebec City area.
Speaking on behalf of all Quebecers, I deplore an attitude that is undemocratic, to say the least, and is a sad reminder of a recent distinction made by Mr. Parizeau between old-stock Quebecers and the others.
Unless Mr. Pelletier withdraws those unfortunate remarks, I urge the Leader of the Official Opposition to dissociate himself from those remarks, in no uncertain terms, in this House where we represent all Canadian citizens.

Mr. Speaker, the National Anti-Poverty Organization has brought forward a study entitled Illiteracy and Poverty which shows a strong linkage between illiteracy and poverty. I want to refer to this report.

Unfortunately despite government lip service to the literacy cause the opposite is happening with economic policies such as the cap on Canada Assistance Plan payments, an additional freeze on health and education transfer payments, cuts to social housing programs and legal aid and the GST.

What is this government going to do to make sure that it attacks the cause of poverty? When you attack illiteracy, you attack poverty.

Mr. Speaker, in a letter to the federal Minister of Finance dated January 15, 1993, the president of the Quebec Bar Association, Paul P. Carriere, made the following comments on Bill C-105, which would amend the Unemployment Insurance Act:
"The changes made in November 1990 to sections 28 and 30 of the act increased the penalties for workers who quit voluntarily without justification or are dismissed for misconduct. Completely excluding from benefits all those who quit voluntarily for a reason that the law does not consider justified or are dismissed for misconduct would be unrealistic in view of the conflicts that arise in labour relations. The measures proposed in Bill C-105 would totally exclude from unemployment insurance benefits thousands of genuine unemployed people, without considering the particular circumstances surrounding their voluntary departure or dismissal for misconduct".

We
recently learned that 81 per cent of university and college women have experienced physical, sexual or psychological abuse within the last year.
Seventy-six per cent of the young men surveyed acknowledged acting abusively to a date. Twenty-nine per cent were sexually abused and 22 per cent were physically abused. There is clearly a need for education so that all people are viewed as full human beings with the right to say no and the right to be treated with respect.
The Secretary of State Women's Program funds many organizations and projects aimed at educating about violence and the rights of women. This program has taken another 10 per cent cut this year and there will be a further 10 per cent cut next year.
February 9, 1993

Anti-racist and aboriginal programs are also being cut during times of growing racial intolerance and in spite of the horrific situation many aboriginal peoples continue to face.
Violence and intolerance grow during bad economic times. Now is not the time-it never is-to cut back on these worth-while projects aimed at strengthening our society.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, within days the main contingent of the 1st Regiment, RCHA will return from its six month tour of duty in Cyprus where both the regular force and militia have served with distinction.
Those who have been a part of this 28-year old peacekeeping operation have every right to be proud, as indeed we are, of their contribution even though the time spent in the observation posts may on occasion have seemed tedious.
Although Canada's role in Cyprus will soon be changing as our troops are needed elsewhere for other UN peacemaking and peacekeeping operations, Canada will likely continue to be a part of an observer force in Cyprus should such be created.
In the meantime, the decision of Canada and some other countries to wind up their activities in Cyprus will hopefully serve to act as a catalyst to the peace talks scheduled for March of this year.
The people of Cyprus, both Greek and Turkish alike, must now find a lasting solution to the division which for too long has tragically divided this island nation.

Mr. Speaker, Canadian municipalities are once again being asked to foot the bill of the government's economic mismanagement. The government is proposing to cut grants in lieu of taxes, resulting in more than $80 million in lost tax revenues for Canadian municipalities.
The government is also proposing to change the formula by which grants in lieu of taxes are calculated, resulting in a loss of several more million dollars for Canadian municipalities.
Mayors from across Canada will be meeting with the Minister of Public Works this evening to voice their concerns over the government's latest attempt to shift the burden of Conservative economic mismanagement on the backs of Canadian municipalities.
Let us hope that the Minister of Public Works will see the error of his government's ways and reverse this unfair and regressive decision. The federal government has a legal and moral obligation to pay its fair share of municipal taxes like the rest of us.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Ontario communities along the Canada-U.S. border welcome Statistics Canada's figures indicating a 15 per cent decrease in same day trips to the United States in November as compared to the same month the year before.
This is good news but to my mind it is no time to back off in our efforts to address this problem. Cross-border shopping is by no means dead.
At Ontario border points there were still 2.2 million automobiles returning on same day trips checked through Canada Customs in November 1992.
All stakeholders must continue to move ahead. For one thing our government must continue to consider the elimination of third party tariffs. Those already removed were well received by the retailers in Sarnia-Lambton and helped lead to lower prices.
A list of further products for tariff removal has been submitted to the Department of Finance. I urge their serious and prompt consideration. I remain convinced that it is initiatives like these that can help our retailers compete on the cross-border front.

Mr. Speaker, the federal government is considering a tax revolt against the villages, towns and cities of this country.

February 9, 1993
In 1992 the federal government paid $420 million in grants in lieu of payments to Canadian municipalities. These payments replaced tax payments for services provided to federal buildings and properties.
It appears the government is attempting to shift its fiscal responsibility to municipal councils and the residential taxpayers will be forced to offset the loss in revenue, estimated to be $80 million over the next two years. There should not be any arbitrary exemptions.
School boards, homeowners and businesses do not get to make their own property assessment. Why should the federal government? The government is considering intrusion into the setting of municipal property tax rates and abandoning a longstanding agreement with the Federation of Canadian Municipalities.
I urge the minister to reconsider any options that would decrease federal fiscal responsibilities to municipalities.

Mr. Speaker, one of the most important concerns facing our nation today is the issue of public security. Canadians from sea to sea are insisting that improvements be made to our criminal justice system. People perceive the justice system as favouring law-breakers instead of supporting victims of crime.
Constituents in the riding of Elk Island question a system that pampers convicts at the expense of victims. Two areas that must be examined are the Young Offenders Act and our parole laws.
The Government of Canada has made some important changes in this regard but more work has to be done. The Canadian Parliament must continue to focus on the issue of public security. Our challenge as a nation is to establish a model of justice that has the support and confidence of all citizens. Let us work together to achieve this important and worth-while goal. Let us all work together for a better Canada.

Mr. Speaker, with Bill C-lll banning the sale of cigarettes to anyone under 18, the government is again showing that it is out of touch and only seeming to govern.
Faced with the big smuggling problem, the government has chosen to attack small convenience store operators and young people instead of the smugglers. Instead of putting its energy into fighting cigarette smuggling, the government's latest effort would impose fines of up to $50,000 on small store owners who dare sell cigarettes to people under 18.
That makes no sense. Who will pay those fines, if not the people, knowing very well that small shopkeepers cannot afford it? It is the same with Bill C-105. The government is attacking the unemployed instead of tax cheaters.

Mr. Speaker, my constituents are concerned that repeat young offenders are flaunting the weaknesses of the Young Offenders Act. Edmonton Sun columnist Linda Slobodian is leading a campaign to get tough on repeat young offenders.
Staff Sergeant Peter Zaharko who heads the Edmonton city police youth unit commented in a recent article by Mrs. Slobodian as follows:
The Young Offenders Act as it stands right now is really a good piece of legislation when it refers to first-time offenders, or really even second-time offenders.
He also notes that it is seriously weak when it comes to repeat offenders. In a survey I did on the Young Offenders Act in my constituency, many of my constituents echoed this view.
I urge the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General of Canada to listen to these views. It is time to get tough with repeat young offenders.
February 9, 1993

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Yesterday, the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Employment and Immigration both said that the 50,000 people who took part in the demonstration in Montreal in -25C weather were separatists. Everyone who opposed Bill C-105 on unemployment insurance reform, even Conservative or New Democratic members, as well as Liberal members and senators, and who participated in the march on Sunday afternoon were called separatists by these two ministers. Does the Prime Minister agree with this rather surprising statement from two of his senior ministers?

Mr. Speaker, I have not read the transcript of the comments in question. I think that the minister said, and it is common knowledge, that Gerald Larose is not a great supporter of my friend or our party or the New Democrats and that his political options are well known. I think that is what was mentioned.
As for the substantive issue, the hon. member simply said that his recommendations were very much like those put forward by the Leader of the Opposition when he was Minister of Finance in 1978. The Leader of the Opposition who was then Minister of Finance found it quite acceptable, and rightly so, because the purpose was to control spending. Is that acceptable? Is it morally acceptable for a government to stop paying unemployment insurance benefits to someone who quits a job without any valid reason or justification? That is the issue. In these circumstances, we come to the conclusion that Canadian taxpayers do not have to pay unemployment benefits to someone who quits a job without just cause. Now, if my friend has a different opinion, he should tell us.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to know from the Prime Minister if he agrees that the tactic of the minister in calling
Oral Questions
everybody who is opposing this bill a separatist is unacceptable to the Canadian people. There are hundreds of thousands of Canadians in every part of Canada who think that some provisions of this bill are completely unacceptable.
Will the Prime Minister agree with me that the only separation I support would be the separation of this minister from his ministry?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is suggesting that the minister be separated from the Crown because he has tightened up on the unemployment insurance requirements.
What would he say then about himself? In 1978, when he was Minister of Finance, he reduced the weekly benefits from 66 2/3 to 60 per cent of weekly insurable earnings.
Oh, oh.

I share the sense of shock of the NDP. What we are dealing with here is that members of the NDP may be opposed to us on the GST. They may be opposed to us on free trade. They may be opposed to us on deficit reduction, but at least they have the courage to have a position, as opposed to the hypocrisy of the Liberal Party who has two positions on every issue.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will quote someone who is neither a separatist nor a socialist. Yesterday, Ghislain Dufour, president of the Conseil du patronat, suggested that the government refer the problem to a committee of the House of Commons and allow public hearings, because the Prime Minister and the minister are trying to give the impression that people who quit their jobs voluntarily are not penalized. That is absolutely false. They have a penalty of 7 to 12 weeks. Why does the government not act on this suggestion from the president of the Conseil du patronat du Quebec?

Mr. Speaker, since the Leader of the Opposition referred to a demonstration in Montreal, perhaps I could refer him to an editorial that appeared in The Montreal Gazette this morning, which says:

February 9, 1993
Oral Questions

"What is frustrating and infuriating, however, is that so many of the angry people badly misunderstand the proposed changes. The misunderstanding has been shamefully fomented, it must be said, by some politicians and union leaders for their own agendas. A staggering number of people think the changes will penalize anyone who quits a job even for an overwhelmingly good reason. In fact, no one who has a good reason for quitting a job will be affected. The new rules are aimed only at people who quit their jobs without cause".
The Montreal Gazette is quite right. It is the kind of action that was taken by my hon. friend when he was Minister of Finance in 1978, which he then supported vigorously in the interests of trying to reduce the deficit and which today, simply because he is trying to be a typical Liberal opportunist, he is now denouncing.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. A month ago the minister blamed the unemployment rate in Canada on the unemployed. He claimed they were going to Florida and spending their unemployment insurance benefits there. Now he blames the separatists for the negative reaction to this policy of punishing Canada's unemployed. Why does the minister not admit that the real problem is the minister and his punitive policies, not the unemployed or the separatists?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member talked about penalizing the unemployed and said that I blamed the unemployed. This is not about blaming the unemployed but about protecting Canadian workers and employers. I was told this morning that the Canadian Federation of Independent Business has just submitted to the Liberal Party the results of a survey of its members across Canada. These results show that 81 per cent of small businesses, the businesses that create jobs and prevent unemployment, support the measures announced in the economic statement made by the Minister of Finance in December.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the minister asked us to provide examples in the House where people who voluntarily quit their job would not be protected.
I would like to give him an example of a woman in metro Toronto, employed by a major corporation, who was sexually harassed by her boss. She had proof. She went to human resources. It went right to the president's office and at the president's door, instead of protecting this woman's right to work without sexual harassment, she was shown the door.
I would like to ask the minister how his law can protect this woman and whether he reasonably expects that when someone leaves a job the employer is going to write: reason for leaving, sexual harassment.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that president did not work for the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
If this lady was met with such rudeness by an employer, she would go down to a CEC office where a sensitized employment agent would deal with the person and ensure that she got her benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Contrary to what these people are trying to spread, fear among women in Canada, they are fully protected under the Unemployment Insurance Act.

Mr. Speaker, Canadian taxpayers paid to send the minister of trade to Washington to tell the Americans to back off from the trade harassment against our steelworkers, our woodworkers, our pork producers and our brewery workers.
In today's media the minister is quoted as saying: "Really the Americans are free traders. Really they are not protectionist. I am coming away feeling very positive. They have positive things to say about our relationship".
While the minister is talking in these loving Valentinelike phrases, in today's Wall Street Journal there is a full page saying that in 1993 the border between Canada and the United States-
February 9, 1993
The hon. member knows the rule about using props or other things to illustrate his remarks. Would the hon. member put his question, please.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that I cannot hold up the full page of the Wall Street Journal that says that the border between Canada and the United States is to be no barrier to trade, about to be erased.
My question for the minister of trade is simply this: when is the minister going to stop being an apologist for the American interests and start standing up for Canadians, particularly Canadian workers?

Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend should indeed table that ad. I looked at the Wall Street Journal this morning and my recollection is that it is an ad from a telecommunications company that says that in future, because of advanced technology and telecommunications, there will not be any borders between Canada and the United States.
Or between Canada and Europe.

Or between Canada and Europe.
I know my hon. friend and I sometimes read the Wall Street Journal together in the morning. Indeed, if that is the ad, then I think my hon. friend has inadvertently misrepresented that ad and misled this House. I know he would want to apologize to the Speaker and to the Minister for International Trade who represented Canada very effectively yesterday in Washington.
Hear, hear.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker.
We have long since had a practice where it is not appropriate to raise a point of order or a question of privilege during Question Period. This can be done later.
Mr. Speaker, I know the Prime Minister knows the rules well enough to follow your ruling and raise this matter if he feels he has one at the end of Question Period.
I will try to do the best I can without coaching.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade with regard to his trip to Washington
Oral Questions
the other day to discuss trade issues with the U.S. administration.
Part of one of the countervail actions against Canada by the United States is in softwood lumber exports wherein the Americans are making the spurious allegation that our raw log exports constitute a subsidy in Canada.
Did the minister raise this specific issue with trade officials in Washington? Did he get assurances from officials in the new administration that our raw log export regulations stand and are not subject to challenge by the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me first correct something that the member for Kamloops just said.
I made very clear in my comments after the meeting that I had with Mr. Brown and Mr. Kantor, I said it is still early days to draw conclusions. I am not drawing any conclusions. I did not go there to pick fights. I also said that it is still too early to draw conclusions. For my hon. friend to immediately draw the conclusion that because I did not bloody someone's nose down there I was falling into the lap of the new administration is totally wrong and he should know that.
As far as the question posed on the softwood lumber issue, yes I raised that with both Mr. Brown and Mr. Kantor. We had a very good discussion. I set out very clearly the concerns Canada has with the actions.
I also pointed out the fact that the price of lumber in the United States market, partly because of the problems we are having with trade between the United States and Canada has doubled and has increased the price of housing by a few thousand dollars and their actions are hurting their own economy.
I told them I thought it was very important that we achieve a long-term resolution of this issue for the interests of both Canada and the United States.

Mr. Speaker, I will give the minister an opportunity to suggest how successful he was in his visit to Washington.
Yesterday U.S. officials called the steel case a train coming down the track. Unfortunately we agree that the American steel workers are the conductors and Cana-

February 9, 1993
Oral Questions
dian steel is riding the caboose. It is going the way of VIA Rail and the caboose is near extinction.
Did the minister proffer a strong case on behalf of Canadian steel yesterday? Did he insist on a sectoral trade agreement? What assurances did he come away with, if any?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, indeed I did raise the question of steel. I said that this was of extreme importance to Canada because of the significance of the United States market to Canada and also the significance of the Canadian market to the United States producers. I said that the two markets were integrated.
I also raised the point of a U.S.-Canada steel accord, as I indicated to my friend in a previous Question Period that I would. He said that he would take this aboard and give me an early response specifically to the request that I made.
Since I know where the U.S. industry is on this particular issue I also raised the importance of getting started on this with a blue ribbon panel to lay the groundwork for whatever options might be possible, including a U.S.-Canada steel accord.

Mr. Speaker, today the members of the coroner's juiy investigating the tragic death of 11-year old Christopher Stephenson did something unprecedented in the legal history of Canada. It issued a statement which singled out the Solicitor General for blunt criticism for his categorical refusal to consider compensating little Christopher's parents for their legal costs of the inquest. The jury specifically stated that it could not conceive of an inquest of this depth and nature without the perspective provided by the Stephensons' lawyer.
Will the Solicitor General now agree to consider a joint federal-provincial package to reimburse the Stephensons for their legal expenses?

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate my hon. friend's question. I am
sure that everyone in this House shares the tragedy the Stephenson family went through.
I have stated since the start of the inquest that I believe the costs of determining cause of death are quite properly a provincial expenditure and that the province of Ontario had carried the case forward in a very extensive manner.
I also suggested last week at committee that I was prepared to have the Canadian Bar Association or an independent body consider the issue as to whether legal costs of such a person should be paid by the municipality, the province or the federal government, to have the question of independent legal counsel, independent opinions brought forward, whether or not the lawyer's bill should be taxed and what is appropriate.
I do not claim to be the fount of all knowledge on this. I made my decision based on what I know about the process at this time. I am certainly willing to put it to an independent review.

Mr. Speaker, this is an independent jury and the Solicitor General has praised it for its work. It has flatly disagreed with both his assertion that the Stephensons did not need independent legal counsel and his decision to deny funding was sensitive, sound and just. Indeed, it found the Stephenson lawyer's involvement indispensable to its recommendations.
I ask the Solicitor General to do the right thing and act on the poignant recommendation: "That the federal government and the provincial government compensate Jim and Anna Stephenson for all legal costs incurred in this inquest".

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a colleague of the bar what my friend must also find interesting and I think there is a question here, is that when the inquest jury made 71 recommendations that particular one was not among the original recommendations. I am prepared to take it into account at this time since it has reconvened and asked the question.
This is a very serious matter and I wish my hon. friend would treat it as such. I am prepared to have all of these issues examined by an independent commission.
February 9, 1993

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister responsible for the Status of Women. Yesterday a study was released which showed that among young university women, 35 per cent had experienced physical assault and 46 per cent had experienced sexual assault since leaving high school.
We have had statistics like this before but they are becoming more alarming. The time has come to address the attitudes and behaviour which allows such assaults and abuse to continue. We support the studies, but the studies are not solving the problem.
What is the government doing to ensure that such abuse will not continue and to drastically reduce this terrible terror women have to endure?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Environment) and Minister Responsible for the Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Environment)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that my hon. colleague and all colleagues welcomed that study which was funded through the family violence program of the Department of National Health and Welfare. For the first time it gives us the kind of in depth information about the experience of the lives of young women at universities.
My colleague, of course, knows the new laws dealing with sexual assault which were passed last year by this House send that very firm message to all Canadians that no means no. We have to ensure that young women use that tool and put forward the proper complaints and that the courts deal with them effectively.
As well, universities could establish, as some already have, protocols which deal with this kind of behaviour in an appropriate way and provide penalties to students who get involved in inappropriate behaviour.
A lot of this requires work at the very early ages by education within the family and again through a number of the initiatives of the family violence program. We have supported work going on in the schools by the Canadian Teachers' Federation and we look forward to doing a great deal more as a result of these efforts.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, it is fine to deal with the courts and relate experiences in the courts. However, only a small percentage of men who commit this abuse are actually charged. We know that abusive behaviour is learned. Therefore, it can be unlearned.
What is the government doing in conjunction with the provinces to ensure that children who are the victims of abuse realize that this abuse is not right and that they do not have to experience and live with it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Environment) and Minister Responsible for the Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Environment)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure my colleagues agree that there is not one simple answer.
It is going to require a multifaceted approach in terms of education which begins at the family level, in the community and in the schools. Young girls and boys have to develop and understand that relations with each other, men and women, have to be on a more appropriate basis. Then it grows from there to the support given by the universities through the counselling services to support women in developing the strength to deal with these situations effectively when they encounter them and to lay and press charges.
All of those factors are moving ahead. The work of the Canadian panel on violence against women is also going to bring forward a national action plan in which we all work together to eliminate this kind of abuse against women.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister of employment.
I have a draft UI document which I would be more than happy to table. It was sent out to the UI offices by the director of benefit entitlement and is full of proposed questions that must be asked of claimants and the reason for all these questions. I quote: "The condition to be met by the claimant in this context is particularly strict and appears to imply that only exceptional circumstances

February 9, 1993
Oral Questions
where the claimant had no reasonable alternative which might have allowed him or her to retain the employment can the immediate voluntary separation be justified". This is clearly a one-sided approach.
How can the minister continue to tell us that his department will give benefit of the doubt to the claimant?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have already indicated that the instructions given to employees of the Department of Employment and Immigration on the application of the Unemployment Insurance Act are being reviewed and new instructions are going to be given out.
Furthermore the training programs being devised for the insurance agents will take into account every possible situation. Ultimately the insurance agent makes the determination.
I remind the hon. member that over four million cases were handled in 1991 by the Department of Employment and Immigration. The vast majority of them were handled with equity and reasonableness and that is what we will continue striving to do.

Mr. Speaker, I am very intrigued by the minister's answer. Clearly we have a case in point that the adjudicator is certainly going to be making the wrong decision.
This morning CBC Radio ran a piece about the dangers of working in the scallop fisheries and how UI would force workers to continue dangerous work. In this radio interview, Lloyd Allen, chief adjudicator for unemployment insurance claims, said that some employment is hazardous by nature and a person would be expected to continue in that employment.
In other words the chief UI claims adjudicator said that quitting a job because of risk of death would not be considered just cause. If that is not just cause, what is?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, how low will they stoop in trying to scare Canadians.
Oh, oh.

To stand on the floor of this institution and tell Canadians that now because of a bill that has
nothing to do with just cause a person cannot quit a job when in danger of imminent death.
It takes only a socialist in a necktie to make a statement like that.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
On Sunday, 50,000 people marched in the streets of Montreal. The government sees it as a separatist plot. I was there, Mr. Speaker. I can assure you these people were not there to talk about independence. They were there for one reason: they want to contribute to the system and not be the eternal victims of that system.
My question is this: when will this government finally understand that the best way to reduce the cost of unemployment insurance is to create jobs, permanent jobs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am really surprised to see the hon. member for LaSalle-Emard, who claims they are going to change the world, object to a measure whose ultimate goal is to break the cycle of dependency that our social security system has generated in this country.
Yes, it is a fiscal measure, but it will also make people more responsible. People who quit their job for a valid reason will be protected. I thought the hon. member would at least admit that and tell these people who were out on the streets that anyone who quits his job with just cause will have all the protection he needs and more, because these people will no longer be penalized as they were before. They will get their full benefits.

Mr. Speaker, the minister said he was surprised to see me there. Well I was surprised that none of his colleagues who opposed the bill had the courage to be there on Sunday.
I ask my question of the Minister of Finance. The problem with unemployment insurance is that this government has no long-term plan to create jobs. Its only policy is to hope against hope that prosperity will spill over the border from the United States.
Just yesterday the Minister of Finance said that he could not proceed with his budget until President Clinton had proceeded with his.
February 9, 1993
Shame.

Mr. Speaker, that is ridiculous. This minister is supposed to be the Minister of Finance for Canada, not the governor of the 51st state.
My question is this. Trickle down meant the end of the road for the Republicans. When will the members-
The hon. member must please put his question.
Mr. Speaker, when will the members opposite realize that trickle north is going to be end for the Tories?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's assertion is absolutely wrong. He knows very well the December 2 economic statement outlined a number of initiatives: investments in people, investments in infrastructure, further investments in international trade, positive steps toward encouraging small business which generates 80 per cent of the new jobs in Canada.
That is reflected in Ottawa Business News, a small business publication which indicated it has become increasingly clear that small business has emerged as the big winner.
This is what Mr. Bulloch had to say about the UI measures. "The UI measures were very significant", Bulloch affirmed, "I've been in the office of Liberal ministers in the seventies and there was agreement that the major area of UI abuse was voluntary quitters. The Liberals didn't want to touch it because it was politically unpalatable".
Well, Mr. Speaker, we did it in the name of fairness.

Mr. Speaker, I too have a question for the Minister of Finance.
I want to ask the minister why is he telling the Canadian provinces to go ahead, prepare and present their budgets now and not wait until after he presents his next budget, when he is saying to Canadians that he has to wait until after President Clinton presents his state of the union message and his first budget to Congress?
Oral Questions
Why does he follow this policy which suggests, like my colleague said, he is acting like the governor of the 51st state instead of the Minister of Finance for Canada? Why will he not present a budget now that will help 1.5 million Canadians get back to work?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what a bunch of nonsense. The provinces can bring in their budgets any time they like. The previous administration used to bring in its budget any time it wanted.
We try to bring in the budget in the spring. We brought down an economic statement in December to keep Canadians and the provinces up to date with respect to the fiscal and economic outlook.
Yes, we will be bringing in a budget. We are listening to some suggestions from across the way as to what might be done and what we might be able to incorporate. So far we have received absolutely nothing in the way of positive recommendations.
I assure the hon. member that I am getting a lot of suggestions from the Canadian people. We will build on the budget of February 1992 and we will build on the economic statement of December 1992.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Finance. He is quoted as saying, after he met with the U.S. secretary of the treasury Bentsen, that they are talking about "providing some stimulus to create renewed economic activity and jobs" and the Minister of Finance then said that it will certainly help Canada.
If the minister thinks that approach is right for the United States, why will he not follow that approach of economic growth for this country? Why does he not present a budget now that will help this country move forward, not backward like his previous budgets?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, welcome to the wonderful world of reality. The United States is our biggest trading partner. As its economy goes, so goes ours. That is a fact of life.
I can tell the hon. member, in case he might be interested, that there was a great deal of interest in the economic statement that I brought down in December. As a matter of fact, I ran out of copies because they were very interested.

February 9, 1993
Oral Questions
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: It was a best seller.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
They were very interested in the balanced approach.
There was the need to contain the deficit and the need to inject some stimulus into the economy. We did both in the December statement.
I remind the hon. member it contained $2 billion worth of expenditure on infrastructure, on training, on the small business sector. Second, it contained $1.8 billion in reduced taxation, something that the Liberals would not recognize.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice. As you know, violence is seen and experienced eveiy day on television, in the streets, in schools and even within our own homes. Recently, one of my constituents was sexually assaulted by an inmate who was out on a day pass. The victim asked for a court order that would oblige her attacker to provide a blood sample, in order to determine whether he was HIV positive or had any other sexually transmitted disease. The judge rejected the application on the grounds that he could not legally accept this kind of application. The judge also indicated that it was up to the legislature to fill this legal vacuum.
I would like to ask the Minister of Justice whether he and the Solicitor General would be willing to make certain changes in the existing legislation in order to give more rights to victims of sexual assault.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Justice, Attorney General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member has raised a rather disturbing point. I think we all understand the concerns of a woman who has been a victim of sexual assault and who has to live with the fear that she may have been infected with a fatal disease. I believe the situation referred to by the hon. member is a very serious one.
However, we must also realize that it is difficult to force people who have not yet been found guilty, against whom charges may be laid, but who have yet to be found
guilty or to plead guilty, to undergo a test that may not fully comply with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member that this matter is being examined by my department, and that, together with my other colleagues at Health and Welfare and the National Advisory Council on the Status of Women, we will see how we can respond most effectively. I can assure the hon. member that I am very much aware of the concerns of the women of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.
On December 7, in his response to the Pearse report, the minister said that DFO is now identifying over-all increases in manpower, equipment and operating funds necessary to ensure an effective enforcement presence during the 1993 season.
Since 1986 DFO's specific region fisheries management budget has declined from 35 per cent to 27 per cent of allocation. Further reductions were made in all departments by Treasury Board in November at a cost to DFO of $12 million so far.
How can the minister possibly keep the promises he made to the west coast fisheries in December?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we will simply spend our money more effectively for a start.
Of course the hon. member is leaving out of account the fact that we have additional funding in connection with our aboriginal fisheries strategy. With that funding, we are entering into co-management agreements. Last year, we had some 80 agreements with the aboriginal bands of British Columbia. Funding is provided in those agreements for habitat enhancement, enforcement and other purposes. We have 60 native guardians who will be getting special training to join our enforcement ranks during the coming season.

Mr. Speaker, the opposition motions reads: "That this House condemns the government for reneging on its commitment to Canadian farmers by changing its policy in the following areas:" and it mentions the Third Line of Defence, the Crow transportation benefit and especially
the GATT agreement that Canada signed many years ago.
For several years, farmers across the country have been very aware of the threat facing them. Over the years, we in Canada have built an agricultural infrastructure that has been very good for our farmers. But with the GATT negotiations, our farmers have been in danger for some time. They know it and they show it. We saw that last year, in February, I think, when nearly
50,000	people came to Parliament Hill to protest this issue of GATT.
But we become increasingly concerned as time goes on, when we realize that the Canadian negotiators in GATT told a parliamentary committee that our position had less and less support in other countries, especially Japan, which wanted to protect its domestic market as we want to protect ours for poultry, eggs and industrial and processing milk.
We are in a situation where our country's negotiators seem concerned about our decreasing support. We are moving towards a new system for which we are not ready and with which our farmers and organizations across the country do not agree.
After this statement by our GATT representative, a small article appeared in the newspapers, reporting that the Minister of Agriculture said that our farm quota system was being vigorously defended. But, Mr. Speaker, we wonder who is telling the truth on this. We are concerned for the simple reason that with the changes imposed by GATT, our farmers' investment in their farms, the family business, if you will, will lose value, that is obvious.
This House even supported and passed a motion asking the Prime Minister to go personally to defend article XI of GATT.
We wanted the Prime Minister to impress upon the European countries, especially upon Jacques Delors, and the newly-elected US President that article XI of the GATT was absolutely fundamental and vital to farmers in Canada. Above all, if I may Mr. Speaker, as I have discovered in my numerous conversations with UPA leaders-that is the Union des producteurs agricoles du Quebec-there is of course a great vested interest, when you think that 48 per cent of industrial milk is produced in Quebec. That is a very important market for our dairy producers in Quebec. But we are very concerned about this change to article XI of the GATT. It would be

Supply
tantamount to revolutionizing the way our producers operate.
They tell us about tariffication. Representatives from Canadian associations, whether from the poultry, egg or industrial milk industry, tell us that they are being pressured into accepting the tariffication instead of the quota system guaranteed under article XI of the GATT. We do not want the tariffication; neither do our farm organizations. I wonder, not so much for myself as for farm associations and organizations of course, who is putting pressure on this country's farm organizations to accept or at least consider tariffication? I thought their answer was pretty clear last year when they rallied on Parliament Hill.
I am sure that, if they could voice their concern in this House, the representatives of all these organizations, especially those from the UPA, they would. They actually did in another way, democratically, through letters, telegrams, petitions and so on. Except that government seems ready to capitulate and see article XI of the GATT fail in the end, and that will have a major impact on agriculture in Canada.
That is why we call upon government. This is very important. We have a motion before us and the Prime Minister has recognized that we have to fight for article XI of the GATT as it affects our farmers, but what we have to do is to stress the importance of having the Government of Canada tell not only European organizations and Jacques Delors, but also the new President of the United States of America that we, in Canada, are not exporters of farm products, that we are in no way destabilizing the global market, that we have no surpluses that could be cause for concern. In that context, it is only normal for the Prime Minister to explain to our GATT partners that it is vital for our country and that we will not accept or agree to sign a deal which will literally drive our farmers to personal bankruptcy.
The situation is very clear, and we would like this government to realize that it has a mandate to protect an agrarian structure that has worked well during all those years, a truly wonderful system for many. I could quote from articles written by U.S. organizations and associations concerning our quota system in Canada. They actually say that they would need such a system, not only for milk, but also for poultry and eggs. If there are people in the United States who believe that our system
is so special, all the more reason for us, here in Canada, to protect this system through our government. But without that will, if it is not made obvious to our GATT partners, of course we will fail.
The message is clear. We have a farming system that many countries wish they had. It is therefore essential that we never agree to abandon a system that has benefited not only our farmers but also Canadian consumers.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say at the beginning of my comments today that I will be sharing my time with my colleague from Winnipeg-St. James.
It is a pleasure for me to make some comments on the motion put forward by the New Democratic Party in condemning the government for reneging on its commitments to Canadian farmers by changing policy in many different areas.
The government should be faulted not only for changing policy but having a number of consultations, and I will give them credit, with many and most of the players in the agrifood industry. However the government has been mostly all fluff and no stuff. However in the major part of the industry many players are now asking where and when is the government going to come up with solutions to all the suggestions and comments that have been given to them.
We know that agriculture in Canada is facing an unprecedented crisis. We all know the economic figures show the primary producer is facing a very uncertain future. It has come to the point where there are even food banks in rural Canada. It is something which has been unheard of and unthought of in the past, but in rural Canada we have food banks.
The average farmer feeds approximately 120 people in Canada. Yet it is very likely that one of the partners in that farm ownership, one of the spouses, is very likely going outside the farm environment and the business environment to work in order to feed that farmer's own family.
What is lacking in this country is a long-term agricultural policy, a long-term vision. We do not have that. We need that. All of us as parliamentarians need to work toward that. I am pleased to say our party in particular has been working very diligently on it and we look
February 9, 1993

forward to unveiling it to the public in the very near future.
The government says it is committed to putting into place permanent safety net programs to get away from ad hoc payments which have been there in the past. I personally have no problem with that but we all know that so far it has not worked. It has been tried. We have all had an opportunity to comment on the attempts that have been made with GRIP and NISA. They are good attempts but they have not worked to the extent that they should and they need a very serious reworking and revamping so that they will.
Agriculture Canada states that in 1992 the total net income in agriculture will be between $4 billion and $4.9 billion. However in 1993 that is expected to drop to $3.3 billion to $4.4 billion. I do not know how successful this government can say it is when the total net income is going to drop to that extent.
In the province of Saskatchewan alone the total income figures last year were between $427 million and $522 million. This year they will be between $250 million and $350 million, down again. How can the government say it has been successful?
This motion before us today deals with several parts of the agricultural industry but not all of them. There is no mention in the motion of a commitment of support for the processing and further processing industries which are also feeling the pinch.
It is a known fact that since 1989 Canada has had close to 100 food processing industries and plants close down. Agriculture Canada figures state there were over 20 such plants in 1989 while five opened, they will admit. According to Agriculture Canada's own figures, unfortunately 34,000 jobs have been lost in the food processing industry.
GRIP and NISA, which are long-term safety net programs, are being tried and are being worked with. So far in many areas they have been insufficient. They have been a disappointment to the farmers and the industry.
It has even gone so far that last week the ministers of agriculture in Manitoba and Saskatchewan made the prediction that these programs would be in such a drastic
Supply
financial situation that by 1995 they might be even too expensive to continue.
Some of the concerns that many of us had when these programs were being discussed in a legislative committee, that they needed to be put in place in a different manner than they were, that they would deliver a fair bit of money in the short term, but in the not too distant future they were not going to be successful, unfortunately I think some of our comments at that time are proving to have been true.
I urge the government to make the necessary changes to those programs so that they can be effective. We had concerns they were not going to be market neutral. Unfortunately those concerns have come true.
The unpredictable prairie weather this year has resulted in a dramatic downturn in the quality of grain produced and therefore the returns to the producers are smaller. In provinces such as Saskatchewan there are estimates that the return, because over 50 per cent of the grain is of feed grain quality, is drastically reduced. The emotional and financial strain on the agrifood industry, in particular on the primary producers, is absolutely incredible.
Other facts and figures we need to consider are these. On the prairies there are more farmers over the age of 70 than there are under the age of 30. We need to consider what we are going to do. I ask this government what it is doing and what is it prepared to do to encourage young people to stay in the industry and to get into the industry.
The third line of defence has turned out to be nothing more than a mythical creature. It was stated that if everything else failed, that the third line of defence type programs would be put in place. I ask the government if this is not the time for that. If there ever was a time that we need third line of defence programs, now is the time. What is the government doing about that? If it is doing anything it certainly has not made it known to the producers.
Producers are getting discouraged. They have lost confidence. They want to know where they are going to go. If we look at what has happened in Ontario this year, I can tell members from very close observation that there are still many acres of com and soybean crops in the fields. I know of one instance where a producer has close to 300 acres of com and soybeans which because of the weather this year was totally written off by crop insurance. Yes, there will be crop insurance payments from

February 9, 1993
Supply
the Canada-Ontario crop insurance program. Here we are today, February 9, and that producer has not received one penny from that program when the claims were put in well before Christmas.
The federal government wants, as it always does, to lay claim to the crop insurance program and the important role it plays. How does it suggest that producer cash flow his business when the crop insurance program does not pay up? I will make just one comment. If the producer was late in paying his or her premium, my guess would be that crop insurance would say: "Sorry, you don't have any coverage".
The other area I want to stress in my last minute is that the government has, as far as I am concerned, let us and the industry down as far as supply management is concerned. I will just close with a couple of comments. How do you think the industry feels when the government's chief negotiator at GATT recently stated basically that the government's position is a lost cause. He then goes on to say that the negotiations are not over yet. I do not know how effective a negotiator he can be.
Perhaps the greatest tragedy is that I do not think the government has recognized to the extent it should the effect this has had and the human tragedy in the rural communities. Farm families just want to be able to continue to work hard for their living and provide good food to Canadians.
Finally, I want to address this to the taxpayers who wonder why governments spend billions of dollars on agriculture. The taxpayer, like all of us in these recessionary times, finds it difficult to rationalize big expenses. Why do we continue to support agriculture? The answer is because it is worth support. The cost of farm support is not cheap but Canadians should ask themselves where they want their food to come from. I believe they want it to come from Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I consider it an honour to take part in this very important debate. It brings to light some of the very serious concerns emanating from my part of the country.
I want to start by saying how disappointed I was in some of the offerings from the other side of the House earlier today in this debate. I paid close attention to the
remarks made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister. One would have to spend a lot of years in this House of Commons to find a more self-righteous, more sanctimonious speech than the one delivered by the hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister. The man stood in his place and talked about how he really cared about the farm community in this country. He talked about how this Prime Minister really cares about the farm community, that there is no greater champion of Canadian agriculture than the right hon. Prime Minister, and he said it with a straight face.
In fact, he told the story about the time when the Prime Minister had lunch with the hon. parliamentary secretary and the Prime Minister did not have his glasses so he borrowed the parliamentary secretary's. What did the Prime Minister say? "When I look through these glasses all I see is wheat". Pretty sanctimonious, selfrighteous stuff.
If you listen to the parliamentary secretary and if you did not know any better, you would think that Canadian farmers had no problems at all. Life is blissful out on the land. In fact, what the parliamentary secretary is saying is that if there are any problems on the farm, if there are any problems in Canadian agriculture, do not blame us. Do not blame the federal government because we have always done our best. We are honourable and we really care.
Let us just look at the record of the government. If we want to talk about the right hon. Prime Minister, we could say that if he really wants something he usually gets his way. For example, take how he went to the wall for the big pharmaceutical companies, the multinationals that want to destroy our generic industry, that want to destroy our compulsory licensing system, a system that prevailed in Canada for 20 years and saved Canadians billions of dollars.
The Prime Minister did not have any trouble going to the wall on that issue. He did not have any trouble giving support to the big multinationals. He brought in Bill C-91 and in the process he destroyed compulsory licensing in the country.
Look at the right hon. Prime Minister's record in the field of agriculture. I will point to a study that was carried
February 9, 1993

out by the Canada Grains Council. We all know how devastating the export enhancement program of the United States has been to grain farmers in Canada. In fact, according to the study carried out by the Canada Grains Council, the export enhancement program cost Canadian farmers between the years 1985 and 1990 something like $2.5 billion. Not a million dollars, $2.5 billion.
One would think that this great champion of Canadian agriculture would be pretty disturbed about that. One would think that this great champion of Canadian agriculture would be down there in Washington shouting from the rooftops. He would be perhaps even trying to throttle the President of the United States for doing such a dastardly thing to Canadian agriculture.
What does the record suggest? What does the record say? The record says absolutely nothing because the Prime Minister says nothing about that. We have asked him for a number of years to address this issue of the Export Enhancement Program. He refuses. The Minister of Agriculture refuses. The entire lot refuses.
They will not do anything. Yet, these are the parrot people who stand in their place and say: "We are the champions of Canadian agriculture. We have a proud record. If you have any problems, don't look at us". I wanted to point that out because we have to get a little balance in this debate. We are not going to allow those people to get away with those remarks.
I want to point to some other things. This government is always so busy, it says, working on behalf of farmers. I will get to some of the problems in a moment. We know the serious problems that farmers face. Yet, this government finds time to be studying the possibility of a North American, continental barley market.
One would think that the government would have better things to do than to be spending its time determining whether there should be a continental barley market. All it has to do is go to almost any farm area of Canada and it will be told in black and white terms: "Forget it. Forget it. We do not want it. It will help only a few farmers near the United States border. It will help only a
Supply
few farmers". In the process, it is one more exercise in the undermining of the Canadian Wheat Board.
This government and this parliamentary secretary stand up and say: "We are the great champions of Canadian agriculture. Just look at us. If you have any problems, please do not blame us".
What does the Prairie Pool say about the continental barley market? I want to refer to a statement that it has distributed. I will mention just a couple of points. I want to quote directly from the document produced by the Prairie Pool: "The CWB pooling system would not survive the loss of the single-desk selling system. If producers have the option of selling to the board or marketing directly to the U.S., the CWB barley pool would become voluntary producers who would have the option to sell only to the board when U.S. spot prices are low. This would depress the pool price and increase the risk of pool deficits. Number two, removing CWB control of sales would affect the board's ability to source grain to meet international commitments".
I could go on and on. Let us face it. What the Prairie Pools are saying makes a lot of sense. You either have a Wheat Board that has some control, or you do not. You cannot have it both ways.
We have to realize just how important the agricultural industry is. For example, it should not be forgotten that the capital value of the agricultural industry right now stands at about $130 billion. If you look at its production of just a couple of years ago, that value had been set at $25 billion. The industry contributed about $10 billion to Canada's gross domestic product.
In fact, that agricultural industry accounts for about seven per cent of Canada's trade. It earns, on the positive side of the ledger, about $3 million. That is the kind of industry we are talking about. We are talking about an industry that is in trouble, an industry that has to be saved and an industry that needs to be supported.
I want to point out in my final remarks that according to the current estimates, income may plummet by almost $1 billion this year on the prairies.
We know this government has done a considerable amount of things in terms of infusing cash into the agriculture industry. We do not deny that for a moment. I know the agricultural industry, especially the producers, are grateful for that. The fact of the matter is that

February 9, 1993
Supply
there is still a cash crisis. Farmers are leaving the land. Bankruptcies are up. There is a lot of despair.
One of the members from Saskatchewan talked earlier today about the number of suicides in his province alone. It gives you an idea of the situation down on the farm. The farmers are asking for about $800 million. It is a lot of money, but we must address that situation. We must address that problem because we have to save the farm and we have to maintain and strengthen rural life.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see that the Liberal member from Winnipeg-St. James has an interest in agriculture and the farming economy and he should be commended for taking such an interest.
I heard him give some recognition to the government for some cash infusion over the past years when the agricultural sector was in some difficulty. If he read local papers-I am sure he has-some Canadians found the cash infusion very significant in terms of paying out from the tax dollars that they put in, many billions of dollars. This averaged I believe $12,000 to $13,000 per farmer per year for the last eight years so I am sure that is what he was referring to. He points out that there is still difficulty in farming, especially in grain farming. He is somewhat critical of the actions taken by this government in trying to find solutions to those problems.
I thought he might have taken some time to put forward a platform as to how his party intends to deal with it as we are going into an election before too long. If he cares to respond to this I hope he does not stand up and say: "We will not do that, and we will not do this, but in fact here are the positive steps we want to take if we form the government". That would be very helpful for this Chamber here today and for the Canadian public because he was somewhat critical of the barley markets that the minister was seeking out.
I cannot imagine why he would be critical of finding and using any effort possible to find new markets for barley as they now have with oats. Since it has been taken out of the Wheat Board, oats are worth more than barley. One cannot necessarily condemn the farmer for wanting to sell it and get a higher price.
With all due respect to his interests, he should not stand and condemn this government, but show me how he is going to get rid of it at a higher price and create markets for the farmer's grain that is going to be produced and has been produced in the past year.

Mr. Speaker, my good friend from Portage-Interlake talks about the infusion of cash into the agricultural community. I repeat that the government-like governments in the past-has contributed in the way of subsidies and other ways toward the agricultural community and that is appreciated.
What is not appreciated is the hypocrisy of the government. I will just point out one example of hypocrisy. I believe the hon. member for Portage-Interlake mentioned the package that was announced two or three weeks ago for the province of Saskatchewan. In that package is $170 million or $180 million. Is that not right?
These people from the other side do not want to point out that that there is only about $20 million new dollars of federal money in that package. It is only $20 million. At the very same time and in the very same year, they cut WGTA payments to the tune of $70 million. For the farmer, regardless of how you cut it, that is a reduction of about $50 million.
In other words, this government gives with one hand and it takes away with the other. In this particular case the hand that takes is taking a lot more than the hand that gives.
That is hypocrisy. That is the kind of policy that this government has been known for for a good long time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Justice, Attorney General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to respond to today's opposition motion, which claims the government has failed to provide clear and unequivocal support for our supply management system. The opposition alleges that the government is sending mixed signals with respect to its position on the strengthening and clarification of GATT article XI.
February 9, 1993

This is patently false. The government has never changed its commitment to strengthening and clarifying GATT, article XI. It has taken a balanced position, and it did so more than two years ago. This position, which was approved by groups of farm producers, groups in the agricultural industry across Canada, has not changed. It was supported across Canada.
The so-called Uruguay round refers to a major series of negotiations which are part of that round and which have been going on for more than six years. One hundred and eight countries are involved. We tend to forget that Canada is one of those 108 countries and that these are probably the most comprehensive and most complex trade negotiations ever conducted in the world.
These negotiations involve an unprecedented number of participants who are more active than ever before. There are many issues on the agenda including agriculture, textiles, subsidies, dispute settlement, access to markets and services, for instance intellectual property, an area in which I had the privilege of working as well, and all other trade related issues.
We must be realistic and consider that when negotiations involve 108 countries at one time, with negotiating committees whose interests do not always coincide, and that when we get into the final stages, the pressure starts coming from all sides. I may say that so far, Canada has fiercely resisted any attempts by partners and allies throughout the world to urge us to drop or modify our position. Our position is clear and has been stated on many occasions.
I think members on both sides of the House will admit-there is no problem on our side-but members on the other side know that we never gave in. In fact, I attended a meeting with the group that represents the largest number of farmers in Canada who are affected by article XI, and I am referring to the dairy producers. They held their annual meeting in Calgary a little over a week ago, and my colleague the Minister for International Trade and I went to Calgary to meet them and discuss and report on the situation in Geneva to show them once again that we want to stay the course and maintain the same position.
What are the chances of success of these negotiations? Despite missed deadlines, dashed hopes and the obvious

This means that the fears expressed many times, especially by the opposition, the same people who from the very beginning opposed freer trade, in particular the New Democratic Party-these people fiercely opposed any change in our economic policies, especially with respect to trade. I think that they should be able to see that the disaster predicted after the free trade agreement was signed has not happened. Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to emphasize that as one of these 108 countries throughout the world that are trying with difficulty, we must admit, but trying nevertheless to have trade rules that apply to everyone efficiently, we have more chance of successfully building our economic future if we prepare adequately to face international trade and prepare to face market rules that will require countries to be more competitive. I would almost say that is a truism. Any attempt to take us back to what it was like 25 years ago or to the market rules of even 10 years ago could hardly work now.
In the supply management sector, which is a rather special case, we have a very real problem. Some countries are saying: "Hey, Canada, you want the best of both worlds! You support free trade, and you want to sell your grain everywhere in Asia, Europe and the United States. You want trade barriers to come down, not just for grain but also for beef, pork and other products, and at the same time you want to protect your dairy farmers, poultry farmers and egg producers who want you to maintain those barriers".
We are often told our position is not consistent. On the face of it, there does seem to be some inconsistency. However, a closer look will show there is no incompatibility, because what we have been doing since GATT first started is adapt our supply management system in accordance with a clear and specific-more or less clear, and I will get back to that-article, the well-known GATT, article XI. What is the underlying principle? It is quite simple. Canada demands the right to say: we have regulated our business sector in these areas across the country. We no longer produce a surplus of milk, powdered milk or poultry. We produce according to Canadian demand, with an extra margin for exports to very minor markets we have been supplying for a number of years. And we also accept certain imports of products that historically have been allowed to come into the country, such as cheese from Europe and certain quantities of yogurt from the United States.
However, under article XI, Canada demands the right to be able to say at the border: we do not send any surpluses to foreign markets, so we have the right under
article XI to prevent other countries from flooding our markets with surplus products that may be dumped at prices that have no connection at all with being competitive or with observing the law of supply and demand.
Until quite recently, article XI had allowed Canadian producers to make a decent living and even enjoy some degree of prosperity, which was agreeable to everyone. However, we had a couple of setbacks, including a GATT ruling, a GATT panel on yogurt and ice cream. We have a problem with the Americans, since the Americans would like to sell their yogurt and ice cream on our markets, and we have high tariffs that prevent the entry of these products. That was challenged at GATT, which said: Canada, you do not have the right or we do not think you have the right to challenge or to prevent entry of these products under article XI in its present form. This caused considerable alarm among our own people who for the past decades had thought they were adequately protected. So what did we do? First, we obtained an agreement from the Americans that there would be no changes regarding yogurt and ice cream for the time being, so that we could continue negotiations at the international level, not just with the Americans but with other countries across the world. This led us to take the position we have now: since article XI in its present form is not sufficiently clear, we request clarification and strengthening of the article so that it covers not just fresh milk, the kind we drink, but also processed milk products like butter, cheese, yogurt and ice cream.
That was the first objective, a very laudable one. I would add that there was a certain, I do not know just what to call it, but in any event, I had a lot of difficulty accepting that the Americans could sell us ice cream or yogurt here in Canada but that we could not sell them ice cream, for example, because they have special permission under GATT. They have special permission from GATT to prevent ice cream from entering their country from Canada, Europe, Australia or anywhere else.
The same goes for the Europeans who over the years obtained a special permission called variable levies giving them a right to impose import duties of whatever amount. I will give you an example. If you take a pound of bacon or a pound of pork to Europe and want to sell it for $2 a pound or $2 for 500 grams, you are refused and the price is raised to $8, if the price in Europe is $8. I think that anyone who takes a close look at that would

Mr. Speaker, it is remarkable to listen to the self-congratulatory words of the junior minister of agriculture. It is such a contrast.

Essex county has some of the best farming country in the world. It has some of the best land in the world. Its climate has ordinarily been excellent for the production of farm products. Yet in Essex county and across Ontario the farm crisis is very real and very serious for many, many Canadians.

We tried to depoliticize and to remove farm support programs from the political process so that there was more predictability about those programs. That was one of the reasons most people wanted to get away from what has come to be referred to as ad hoc programs, programs that come up on the spur of the moment to address a specific need.
The whole idea of GRIP and NISA was to make them predictable so that before you went to the field in the spring to seed your crop you could go to your banker with the program in front of you. You and your banker could be quite certain of the kind of revenue you could generate from each acre of land you were going to seed that spring as opposed to, in some cases, as has been in the past, not knowing how much you get until you finally get an envelope in the mail and you open it. The whole idea of those programs was to make them predictable.
