Let me address the motion. There is no question there are problems in agriculture. There are substantial problems in agriculture. They are largely rooted in the fact that this industry produces a surplus in Canada because of the way we can produce and how competitive we can be and the fact that we have a large land base and relatively small population. As an industry, we have to export about one-half of what we produce. In other words for every dollar a Canadian farmer earns about one-half of that comes from exports. We then are very dependent on the export market. What goes on internationally has a very great effect on what happens to Canadian farmers.
Again, I come back to the NDP and its policy of tearing up the free trade agreement and not wanting to have anything to do with some of the international agreements that are going to provide some certainty.
When we are so dependent on exports and with a relatively small population it is very important that we trade on the basis of rules, with some predictability and reliability, so that we do not have to deal with the Americans and the Europeans on the basis of whims. In many cases they can act like bullies and that is what has been happening in international trade and agriculture. Because of their size and because of the lack of international rules they have been able to essentially make up the rules as they go along. The free trade agreement with the United States puts a stop to that.
As a result of the free trade agreement there is a way of settling disputes. If the Americans disagree with our trading practices or if we disagree with their trading practices we can take the matter to an international court which settles the dispute on the basis of an agreed upon set of rules: the free trade agreement.
How does that work for us? We have had three disputes to date, one of them to do with hogs and pork. We have essentially won in both those cases, although we will call it one dispute. We have won to the extent that the Americans collected tariffs from us. They were asked and are in the process of refunding $26 million or $27 million collected as tariffs that the dispute settlement
mechanism found were not proper. They are being refunded.
We also won a case to do with raspberries, interestingly enough on today of all days. The Americans have been complaining about Canadians selling wheat into their market unfairly. We established a panel under section 18 of the free trade agreement. They came forward with their findings. We won. We essentially had the practices of the Canadian Wheat Board vindicated by the free trade agreement. We had a panel of five individuals, three Americans. We loss the toss and it was an American who chaired it. By the way, a former justice of the Supreme Court of Canada and a former attorney general of the United States sat on it. It was a pretty high powered group.
They essentially found that Canada was complying with the free trade agreement on five counts: that the acquisition prices of goods referred to in the relevant article include only the Canadian Wheat Board's initial payment; that only storage and handling charges paid by the board should be included; and that the Western Grain Transportation Act should be excluded from the calculations. We also won in two other areas. We won in the sense that we have had the practices of selling into the United States vindicated by a process established under the free trade agreement.
If we listen to members of the NDP, they are going to tear that up. That is not a very smart thing to do if they are going to stand up and advocate policy on behalf of Canadian farmers.
Let me give the results of what has happened in the last three years. Since the free trade agreement has come into effect we have had three complete crop years. The crop year runs from August 1 to July 31. It is different from a calendar year or fiscal year. They have gone from about 1.68 million tonnes to about 3.25 million tonnes. It is almost a doubling of exports into the United States, quite a remarkable record when we think about it.

I understand that there are applications and discussions with the government having to do with importing tomato paste and the possibility of making other products such as juices, ketchup and other things.
What happens to the Canadian grower? The Canadian grower then is cut out of that process. In other words, a lot of paste imported from Mexico and the southern United States would go into a Campbell plant in the Toronto area to be processed into ketchup, tomato juice and other products. Therefore, the long and short of it is that the Canadian farmer is cut out of that industry.
I see my time has come. I will give the rest to my colleague.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too am very pleased to be able to rise in the House today to speak about an issue that is always very dear to me and of concern to us. We share that concern with the producers of agricultural products right across this country and the processors of those products. The entire sector includes the major producers on the farm, through the processing plants to the consumer. We have to think of all of those people when we talk about food in this great country.
We also must recognize we have always had the ability to produce high quality foods much beyond the capability of our domestic consumption. We have always had to depend on export markets for those extra dollars that are so necessary to keep agriculture going. I know some provinces probably export 80 per cent of what they produce in the grains and oilseeds sector in particular, so that does cause an extra drain when it comes to difficult times. As times become more difficult we have a tendency to produce more to try to make up for the shortfall we have had in income.
This year we have been extremely challenged right across the nation because of the devastating weather effects we have experienced. In August of this year Alberta experienced snow and frost, which is a very unusual situation. In my province of Ontario we have had similar situations where the corn did not mature.
The Essex-Kent area of my hon. colleague suffered a severe drought last year although this year the crops were better. This year in other parts of the province we have all experienced an extremely wet summer and lack of maturity of crops. We usually produce top quality corn, capable of being used for distillers, the com sweetener plants, et cetera. This year the value of that commodity is somewhere in the number five grade, which is only fit for livestock feed and the keeping qualities of it are not as good.
We know we have to try to work with organizations and companies to find markets for that com because we want
Supply
to clean it up this year. We do not want to carry it through to another crop year and create problems then.
Despite all that, some sectors of the agrifood industry in Ontario have had some growth. There was a 28 per cent or $544 million increase in the value of those exports in 1992.
I will give you another example. Just last week the Canadian Embryo Exporters Association announced that Ontario breeders would be exporting bovine embryos to Japan, making Canada the first country to break into that Japanese market. At home, the dairy industry is strong and stable and beef prices have continued to rise.
It is high time that has happened because we have not seen a decent beef price for many, many years.
The Ontario average net cash income per farm before depreciation has shown a slight decrease from $21,592 in 1987 to $21,053 in 1991. That does not take into account any off-farm income.
I know some of the speakers have alluded to statistics that show off-farm income has been added but those figures do not include the off-farm income. Moreover, Ontario farms are holding their value. The net worth of the average Ontario farm has increased in the last four years from almost $395,000 in 1987 to almost $522,000 in 1991. That is an average annual increase of 8 per cent.
In 1991, the average equity held by Ontario farmers was 85.1 per cent. The proportion of Ontario farms with high debt loads and low cash flow has decreased in the last five years. In 1991, 7 per cent of farmers had less than 75 per cent equity and less than $20,000 in cash flow, down from 13 per cent of farmers in 1987.
Industry debt is now better held by those able to service it. In 1987 on average, Ontario farms with over $20,000 in cash flow carried 63 per cent of the debt. These farms carried 76 per cent of the debt load in 1991.
Debt is not a universal problem in the farm sector. Thirty-six per cent of Ontario farms reported no debt interest payments in 1991 compared to 26 per cent of Canadian farms. The outlook for the industry is still good.
Total cash receipts from Ontario agriculture for 1992 are expected to increase between 8 per cent and 10 per cent from 1991 to between $6 billion and $6.1 billion.

Total cash receipts for 1993 are expected to range between $5.6 billion and $6.1 billion.
Ontario agriculture is holding its own. At the same time, we realize there are some real problems in the industry. I have alluded to those problems before and most of them this year have been caused by the weather, compounded by the low prices of commodities over the last few years.
During the past year, for example, some farmers saw significant yield and quality loss to their crops because of the poor weather. The safety nets the government developed jointly with the industry and the provinces are attempting to address that situation.
In 1992, federal and provincial safety net program payments to Ontario farmers are expected to be between $633 million and $744 million. Because of the difficult growing and harvest conditions this crop year, the federal government in December announced emergency cash advances of up to $15,000 in unthreshed grain.
That program was not taken up to a great extent because of the unusual weather conditions we had in late December and again in January. It is the first time in my farming history that I can recall when the combines were out very close to Christmas and again in January harvesting corn that we had not anticipated would be harvested until spring.
We are fortunate in that way. We have to recognize the quality of that commodity. As I said before, it was not great but at least it gave some of those people the opportunity to get that commodity off the fields and be in a better position in the spring to get on with their planting for 1993.
We are eternal optimists and believe if we can get another crop in the ground, the next year is going to be better. I have farmed all my life and I guess that is how I think as well. By working together and trying to resolve the problems we have come through, we can achieve those things.
In addition, GRIP, the Gross Revenue Insurance Plan interim payments cheques totalling more than $96 million of which $39 million was for corn have been mailed to more than 25,000 farmers, including nearly 1,800 corn producers who are covered under that program.
There is also a projected $39 million to go out in April of this year to the farm sector. In October or November of this year the balance of that GRIP payment of $45 million will go out as well. A total of $180 million will be going into the farm sector for that crop year.
Since 1985-86 the federal government has spent more than $4 billion in support in the agrifood sector. This works out to about $7,000 per Ontario farm annually. About 60 per cent was direct income support to fanners. The other 40 per cent was used to fund research, inspection, marketing and trade activities, transportation, rural development and operating costs.
Through partnerships with the Ontario government and producers we will continue to provide those safety nets which allow farmers to ride out tough times. Meanwhile, the federal government is working hard to develop trade opportunities and a competitive business environment so that Ontario agriculture can continue to thrive in international markets.
As the minister and others spoke earlier, there are the long-term plans for agriculture that farmers can rely on and the continuity of present programs that were started by the former Minister of Agriculture and Deputy Prime Minister. Everyone is familiar with the "Growing Together" paper which I was also involved with. It is the most comprehensive agriculture plan we have had to develop in many, many years.
That is because things have changed throughout the world and not just in Canada. It is a universal market and we have to compete in it. The U.S. farm bill of 1985 or 1986 has certainly changed the atmosphere of how we trade. We have done the best we can to compete and meet markets wherever we could. Of course, we brought in GRIP, NISA and crop insurance. We have tried to create those programs to sustain agriculture through those lows experienced this year.
It is unfortunate some Canadian producers chose not to buy into GRIP or crop insurance. It is a voluntary program and it was the choice they made. It is unfortunate that they do not have some of that protection.
Granted, the programs are probably not perfect but they are the best we have for today. We have to continue and as times change and as markets change we respond to the world and Canadian demands to put programs in place. With the dollars we have to work with we have to

stay within a budget and we have to put money into sectors the farming community believes necessary. Everyone in this House knows the situation of the debt, not only of this government but also the debts of provincial governments. Therefore we have to work only with existing dollars.
We have worked very closely with farm organizations across this country for many years. I know the previous government did as well prior to 1984. As I have said, circumstances have changed so much that we have had to come up with new ideas. I think everyone in this House has good ideas on how to develop programs but it is very difficult to know what to do in a situation such as we are facing this year with limited dollars.
Farm organizations and individuals who served on committees with great ambition have tried to help the farming sector in providing the tools to work with. We have tried to put a program in place whereby before a producer goes to the field in the spring he can predict a minimum amount of acreage payment. That should give some comfort to both the lender and the borrower. We hope there will be greater participation next year.
We have also introduced legislation, Bill C-54 I believe, and we hope to get that through the House fairly quickly. We feel that would help producers in the longer run with development and promotion of their products and buying Canadian.
The Farm Credit Corporation legislation has had first reading in the House and we hope it will pass fairly quickly also. Most people in this House have had the opportunity to examine that legislation. I believe it is another tool that the agriculture sector will be able to work with, with the extension of lending beyond the farm gate to farm related business. As well it will help with the generation of transfers.
We are trying to work with existing programs. We also are working continually in trying to streamline our export programs so that if we have an opportunity to make an agricultural sale we can put the export credits in place much faster. We have to be very cautious when we do those things. All of those things are hopefully helpful.

We can understand why provinces are reluctant to give in some of their cases, but those are areas where we have to work together and see if we can smooth the trade problems we have and the irritants within our country.
Another area that we feel very good about and we think is necessary and should have been done years ago is the placing of qualified persons in our key embassies around the world who can talk about agriculture and thereby put us in a better position to talk about the food services industry and the things that we have to offer to the people of Canada.
I am quite prepared to give up my time now. I will take questions for a few moments, but I want to make sure the member from Greenwood has the option to make some comments as well.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to respond to the member's comments, particularly about the "Compare the share" of the hon. member for Lambton- Middlesex. I know he has done a lot of work in this area and has travelled across Canada as well with that message.
No matter what the situation, we always feel that someone else is making more than we are. I believe in the situation that from the farm gate this does happen. He mentioned the example of wheat. That included the box in the value of the wheat.
We wish that was double. You would think that somewhere there would be room to double that. I do not know but I understand that is a very competitive market. If we could find a way of doing that, I do not know how much more wheat we would produce in this country. It is an area that is of concern to all of us. With regard to the quality of food in Canada, we have always prided ourselves on the food that we have. Any food that is imported, everything that comes in here, is high quality food. I believe the Canadian consumer has been protected and assured of high quality products when he or she goes to the store to purchase products.
He talked about an article on contaminated birds. I do not know the substance of the article or anything about it. I do not know of any food chain in Canada that could afford to take any risk with food that did not meet Canadian standards. We have always felt our fast-food outlets in Canada have been extremely good and we have had virtually no problem with any food contamination. I believe that is because of the standard we have set and the inspection system that we have as well.
I believe that we have been competitive because of the high quality that we have and we intend to maintain that high quality.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. parliamentary secretary a question with respect to the Canadian Wheat Board.
The Canadian Wheat Board, as the member will know, is something that is very near and dear to the hearts of western Canadians. As an institution, it is very popular and has done a great deal of good for western Canada over the last number of decades. In fact, the support for the Canadian Wheat Board became very clear at the recent rally that took place in Saskatoon when one of the speakers made the comment: "Please don't touch our Canadian Wheat Board". That comment received a standing ovation from 13,000 farmers. It is a very popular institution.
One comment that I get time and time again from farmers is if the government is going to make changes to the Canadian Wheat Board, will it at least put it to a vote. The reason is that the Canadian Wheat Board is paid for by farmers. The government does not contribute except at times when there is a pooling deficit. It is an institution that is for farmers, to represent farmers, and farmers are saying that the government should not be ramming changes down their throats. If there are going to be changes, there should be a vote.
Right now there is a study on the future of barley and a report will be issued. I wonder if the parliamentary secretary can help me and farmers across western Canada. If when that report comes down it suggests that barley be removed from the Canadian Wheat Board for the North American market, can the member assure this House and Canadians right across the country that before any changes to the Canadian Wheat Board with respect to barley, there will be a producer vote. Can the

member give some comments with respect to that? That is something I am hearing, something that farmers want. Certainly farmers would like to hear some definite answer from the member if he can give it.

Mr. Speaker, I would not want to prejudge a report before it comes to us as to the future of any recommendations concerning the Wheat Board and barley. It is not a government board, but we are responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board in any pool deficit and other similar things that happen. They have had their work cut out for them in these areas and challenges have been there too. It has not been easy trying to compete in a market where it is being subsidized with many dollars in a traditional market for Canadians.
We are very proud of the agreement Hon. Alvin Hamilton made years ago with China which was a very beneficial market for Canada for many years. We just wish we could continue to find more markets that would give us the continuity and the projections that one did. There was a lot of security in that as well.

The House resumed from Tbesday, November 24, 1992, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fee that Bill C-305, an act respecting the award of the Victoria Cross, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Departmental envelope.

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to finally speak on this bill standing in the name of my colleague, the hon. member for Red Deer. Bill C-305 proposes to reinstate the award of the Victoria Cross. It seems to have taken a long time to get to this point.
The Victoria Cross is the highest decoration that can be awarded by the British Empire to any member of the navy, army or air force, from the highest to the lowest ranks. This bronze cross, bearing the British lion above

Private Members' Business
the Crown of England and the words "For Valour", takes precedence over all other British orders or decorations.
Since the Crimean War, the Victoria Cross has been the Commonwealth's premier military decoration. It was a great honour to receive this decoration during the Second World War because only a very small number of crosses were awarded.
We are an independent nation, but we have no distinctive military decoration to recognize exceptional bravery by our soldiers in the face of the enemy.
This decoration is older than the Dominion of Canada. In fact, it was instituted by Queen Victoria in 1856. Among the first recipients was a Canadian, Lieutenant Alexander Robert Dunn. Over the years, Canadian recipients have totalled 93, including 10 Quebecers.
In 1972, we decided to create our own Canadian decorations and medals. However, we still have no decoration which recognizes acts of exceptional bravery. The government is now examining this situation.
The Victoria Cross is important because there is a proud tradition in this country, a military tradition, that most Canadians do not know or understand. Canada is a peace-loving nation. We have never initiated a war and, God willing, we never will.
Nevertheless, on several occasions, we have answered the call to arms in defence of liberty and freedom. We still have brave, courageous men and women in this country who even today serve under the flag of the United Nations, proudly wearing the Canadian flag on their shoulders.
These Canadians are prepared to endanger their lives and act very bravely for peace and freedom in far-off lands.
Nevertheless, for Canadians serving in the armed forces today, the highest military distinction ever awarded to Canadians does not exist since it has not been recognized in Canada's system of decorations and distinctions.
In resuming this debate, I ask the government to consider Canadians' request to respect our military tradition and create military awards that recognize the bravery and courage of our service people.
In closing, I ask that the Victoria Cross again be awarded to our heroes.

Mr. Speaker, I feel privileged to rise in the House to address the private member's bill put forward by my colleague from Red Deer.
I regret that I did not have the opportunity to speak before at different times and in different circumstances. However I am privileged and honoured to speak because this is a subject dear to the hearts of many Canadians. I know it is dear to the hearts of many veterans in my riding.
Because it is a private member's bill, members have been allowed to express their views without the concern of following party lines or following instructions from the Whip, the House leader or anything of that nature. I am glad it has taken on the position of a private member's bill.
We all know the history of the Victoria Cross. We studied it in books in school. Some of us have had the privilege of knowing Victoria Cross winners. In my particular case I am very proud to say that I have known four Victoria Cross winners, and two of them very well. I notice a number of things when I am in the presence of those who have the honour of having been awarded the Victoria Cross.
The Victoria Cross is the highest award for gallantry in the British Empire. It was conceived and put together in 1856 by Queen Victoria. It is known throughout the world. It has universal recognition as, if not the, certainly among the highest award for gallantry in the world. If it could be recognized in the universe, I would be so strong as to say that it could be recognized universally.
Since the Victoria Cross was initiated by Queen Victoria in 1856, it has been awarded to very few people. In fact the first Canadian to be honoured with this award was in the Crimean War for his part in the charge of the famous light brigade in the battle of Balaklava. Since the award to Lieutenant Alexander Robert Dunn, the first Canadian to receive this award, 92 other Canadians have been given it.
It is not parenthetic to say that the award is given for the most conspicuous gallantry in the face of the enemy. There have been occasions when the award has been
February 9, 1993

bestowed not in the face of the enemy but these are very few and far between. Some of the 93 Canadians earned this award posthumously.
If we speak to any military man, any military woman or military family and mentioned the name of the Victoria Cross, we see the response of reverence and dignity that it brings.
Canadians became ineligible for this award when Canada developed its own system of decorations and awards in 1972.
I suppose one could hope that Canadians would never be asked to fight in a skirmish like World War I, World War II, Korea, the Crimean War where the award of this decoration would be necessary. In our recent past, and as recent as the Falklands campaign, the Victoria Cross was awarded to those who were involved in the battle and showed conspicuous gallantry in the face of the enemy.
I believe that most members who have spoken have generally spoken in favour of it. I can understand why they would. They would for the reason that I am, because of the universal dignity and honour it brings.
There are some difficulties in having a Victoria Cross eligible for award to Canadians. I do not think any of these obstacles are insurmountable. I understand we will not be able to talk out this private members' bill, and neither should we because of the importance of it.
If it is the intention of this court, the highest court in the land, to move forward with the private members' bill there are ways around the difficulties. I have been told there are ways that would not infringe on the rights of the Sovereign. This would be a concern from the viewpoint of the Secretary of State since it is a medal for the British Empire and is conferred by Her Majesty the Queen.
I use as a precedent the Australian situation in which that country decided to adopt the Victoria Cross as its highest military decoration. However its government did not proceed by legislation. Instead, Her Majesty was asked to issue a letters patent signifying her will and pleasure that the Victoria Cross in this case for Australia, would be the country's highest declaration and that its award would be governed by regulations that her staff had set out in the schedule.
Private Members' Business
Her Majesty also agreed that the Australian Victoria Cross itself should be identical to the original. I think it is important so that the universal recognition factor would pertain.
In addition, some of the other provisions were stipulations that award of the decoration should be made with the approval of the Sovereign by instruments signed by the Governor General of Canada, in this case, on the recommendation of the Minister of National Defence.
There has to be some staff work done to accomplish this. However it is my belief that should this House vote in favour of retaining the Victoria Cross, which would be awarded for conspicuous gallantry, the highest gallantry in the face of the enemy, then I believe the same mechanism could be applied.
The Victoria Cross could then become Canada's highest military declaration without fear of degrading or otherwise qualifying those Canadian decorations like the Meritorious Service Cross, the Award for Bravery, the Cross of Valour and the other Canadian decorations that we now have.
I do not see it in any way, shape or form qualifying the national system we have had in place. It has been evolving since 1972 and is a very appropriate and fitting complement to this award.
In conclusion, I would say that I represent those veterans who I have spoken with and non-veterans. I have discussed this with at least two Victoria Cross winners and they are certainly in favour of it. I understand why they would be.
I will tell the House something that is rather unique in this case. It is unique that it is a private members' bill and I do not have to worry about how my party is voting. It is also unique that I have not spoken to one person who has had difficulty with this. When you come down to the crunch, providing it could be done without changing the qualification of the other series of decorations and awards, no one has any great difficulty with having an award that is as universally recognized as the Victoria Cross.
I speak in favour of this motion. I would like to take the opportunity to congratulate the member for bringing this to the floor of the House of Commons. I know the difficulty inherent in stick-handling a private member's bill through and I do congratulate him on it. I know that, certainly from my viewpoint and that of other members

and constituents and Canadians I have spoken with, they would generally be in favour of this motion. I will support this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to make a brief intervention and, I hasten to say, an intervention in favour of the intent of this bill. In doing so I want to pay tribute to my colleague from Red Deer who has introduced the bill and, as his hon. friend indicates, stick-handled it very skilfully along the way.
I think it is important that we restore the Victoria Cross to its place at the top of the military honours list for this country, a place that it had for a considerable length of time. I think it is important that we do this. It is important that we in this way pay respect to those who have served our country in a number of wars in a number of theatres.
Within this House we still have members who served actively during the Second World War. I commend the member for Regina West who was one of those people as well as our member from Burlington and the member from Athabasca who served during the Korean conflict. I am sure there are others. I do not mean to leave them out. I think it is important that we recognize the kind of contribution and the kind of sacrifice they have made so that people of my generation have been able to enjoy a lifetime free of those concerns and free of having to make that kind of sacrifice.
I simply want to lend my support as a prairie member and as a member from Saskatchewan in support of the spirit and intent of this private member's bill which would restore the Victoria Cross and make it the medal awarded in this countiy as the highest honour for exceptional valour. I commend my colleague from Red Deer.
